blog_personal_01_luna.text:
Our 10 day potty training experience (but only after 3 other terrible methods!)

Our 2 years 9 month old Maya had her birthday on May 14.  By June we were ready to kill someone...

We'd tried sticker chart (she didn't care).  We'd tried letting her run around naked (3 puddles on the rug!) We'd tried the 'nice' weekend approach (a lot of prompt which made her hide behind the couch everytime we talked about the potty!) 

So on the home stretch in Sacramento on the long weekend June 7-16, we started to think of potty training as not like a test she needs to pass, but something she learns to do.

1st Day: Stop using diapers all together in the day.  (We bought 6 pairs of cheap cotton underwear.  Maya picked the purple ones.)  We put the little floor potty in the bathroom.  We put a waterproof mat under the potty.  We calmly said every 45 mins. "It's potty time".  No asking if she has to go.  No arguing if she didn't want to do it.  Just try again later.

Key: We let her OWN it.  She brings her underwear to the laundry basket herself.  She flushes the potty by herself.  She gets to pick 1 little reward from the treasure box for successful potty trips.  Usually temp tattoo or plastic animals under $2.  Accidents were boring and matter of fact.  "Pee goes in the potty.  Let's clean it up".  Nothing shaming, nothing lecture. 

Day 3, 4 were tough.  We had 6 accidents on Monday.  One was at the library.  East Sacramento.  I was ready to quit.  But our pedi had told us expect inconsistency in the first week.  So we kept going.

Day 6: Maya can now go 2 hours dry.

Day 8: She said "I have to poop" and made it to the potty in time.  Marathon finish line.  Yeah!

We still used diapers for nap, night time.  Night time dryness is a developmental thing on it's own.

Day 10: She can do potty in the day.  Even if we go to the grocery or McKinley Park.

The key to this process (and it wasn't perfect) was... consistency.  Less words.  Lower expectation.  Let her OWN the process.

How we potty trained our toddler in 10 days (after 3 methods that totally bombed) 
 On May 14th, our daughter Maya was 2 years, 9 months old. In June, we were in a bad way. Sticker charts she wouldn't use. Running around naked (ended up with 3 puddles on the rug). This "gentle weekend" method of constant prompting she was starting to hide behind the couch when we spoke of the potty (sooooooo many prompts!) 
 During a long weekend (at home in Sacramento, June 7-16) we did a shift - from potty training being a test to pass, to being a thing to learn. 
 Day 1. No diapers during the day. Just all done.  Bought 6 pairs of cheapo cotton underpants. (Maya picked the purple pair.) And a tiny floor potty in the bathroom. Underneath it, we put a waterproof mat.  We told her "it's potty time," every 45 min. (Just calmly, no "do you need to go?") If she resisted, we weren't pushy. "Oh well, let's try again." 
 The key element - ownership. She put her own underpants in the laundry. She flushed the toilet. She got to pick one little reward from the treasure box after each successful trip to the potty (usually a temp tattoo or <$2 plastic animal). Accidents were "No big deal. Pee is supposed to go in the potty. Let's clean it up. Boring." No scolding, no preachiness. 
 Days 3 and 4 were rough. 6 accidents on Monday. (East Sac library!)  I almost gave up, but our pedi said it's normal for the first week to be wacko. So we kept going. 
 Day 6 - she's going 2 hours at a time. Day 8, she said "I gotta poop" and made it to the potty in time. Felt like winning the marathon. 
 Diapers for nap, at night. Dryness at night is a different developmental thing. By day 10, she's reliably using the potty during the day (even when we go to the grocery store. Or to McKinley Park.) 
 Not a perfect method we did to get it to work. But more consistency. Less talking. Reasonable expectations. Let her feel it's hers.

blog_personal_03_glm.text:
Grading papers instead of billing. First semester of teaching 
 In August 2023, I left Hendricks & Cole.  After 14 years as a corporate attorney, I was off to Room 214 at Roosevelt High School.  Provisional teaching license in hand.  Ready to die of fear.  My 42nd birthday in October was the first I'd had in a decade where I wasn't responding to emails on my phone. 
 Why did I do it?  Why?  Well... I defended a merger in 2022 that cut 300 jobs in a town of 8,000.  I couldn't stop thinking about it.  My sister's a 4th grade teacher in Duluth.  Been at it 20 years.  She said, 'You're always thinking about the cost.  Think about the value instead.' 
 So, here's a peek at my first semester of teaching 11th grade civics and one section of Constitutional Law.  Yes, we have it in our district. 
 I get paid $52,400 a year.  2019 I was earning that by March.  But I've never eaten a meal at my desk.  Also, I stopped taking migraine meds in November because...*fingers crossed*...I no longer need them. 
 Man oh man, was I in over my head.  Yale law. Big law.  12 years.  I thought classroom management would be 'leadership skills'.  Well....it isn't.  Didn't realize that I would not get my 3rd period (31 sophomores) to settle until late September unless I let Marcus lead with his 'news of the day' summaries.  Now it's the highlight of my mornings. 
 Hardest week so far.  October 16.  I was there late for parent/teacher conferences.  And 6 parents, some askingly, asked me why I wanted *their* kids.  Truth?  Because a kid named Priya in my 2nd period civics asked if the First Amendment applies to her Tiktok.  It's the best question I've been asked in a long time. 
 Last day of finals was December 20th.  I closed the grade book.  84% of my students passed.  One student named Diego wants to be a lawyer now.  I didn't cry.  Almost though. 
 My bar card is still in my wallet.  Old dogs, eh?  But tomorrow, when the bell rings at 7:45.  I'll know where I'd rather be.

No billable hours. Grade Papers instead. First Semester.

Last August, I left Hendricks & Cole (after 14 years as a corporate lawyer) and entered Room 214 at Roosevelt High School with my provisional teaching license and overwhelming fear. I'm 42. In October. It was the first birthday in ten years I didn't open my phone to check emails.

Why did I quit? 2022 I defended a merger that axed 300 jobs in a 8,000 person town. Couldn't shake it. My sister's a fourth grade teacher in Duluth for 20 years. She said "You always calculate costs. Try to calculate value."

Here's what it's been like to teach 11th grade civics and one section of Constitutional Law (Yes! We have it in our district).

I'm earning $52,400/year. I had that by March in 2019. I've never eaten dinner at my desk. I stopped my migraine medicine in November. Knock wood!

I've had a rude awakening in the learning curve. Twelve years in Yale Law/Big Law. Classroom management is just "leadership skills." It's not. It was late September before I realized my 31 sophomores in 3rd period only shut up if I let Marcus start the class with "news of the day" every day. It's the highlight of my mornings.

Worst week? October 16th. Staying late for parent teacher conferences. Six parents wanted to know - some curiously - why a lawyer would be interested in *their kids*? I told them: Because the girl in my 2nd period Civics class (Priya). She asked me "Does the first amendment cover my TikTok?" That's the best question anyone's asked in years.

Final Exams finished 12/20. I closed the gradebook. 84% of the kids passed. I had one kid (Diego) tell me he wants to be a lawyer. I almost cried.

I still have my bar card in my wallet. Old habits die hard.

But at 7:45 tomorrow morning when the bell rings. I know where I'd rather be.

blog_personal_05_sonnet.text:
Flew into Kansai Tuesday in October, capped spending at $100/day(15k yen/day). Headed out and thought Kyoto was one of the more straightforward cities to do this in. You're just replacing cabs with a bike and Michelin with tofu joints. 
 - DAY 1  Haidaikyu hostel near Kyoto station. 3400 yen a night for a dorm. Got icoca card at station kiosk 
 - Bicled (rented bike from hostel, 800 yen/day) instead of buses. Kyoto is super flat. You see bike lanes everywhere. 
 - Breakfast was a coffee/pastry from Lawson konbini (450 yen). 
 - Went to Fushimi Inari before 8am(just beat the tour buses). Gates are free. You can walk to Yotsutsuji overlook in 40mins. 
 - Lunch at standing soba place near shrine (600 yen, kitsune soba) 
 - Afternoon at Tofuku ji(500 yen to get in to see the garden) 
 - Bicled over to Gion. Walked around(free to walk Hanamikozy or sneak into Yasaka shrine. Free) 
 - Dinner, a bowl of ramen at a counter place in pontocho(900 yen). Got can of asahi from vending machine(150 yen) 
 - Total for the day 10200 yen (ish). Under budget. 
 DAY 2 
 - Passed on hostel breakfast. Got onigiri from konbini (300 yen) 
 - Bicled to Arashiyama for the bamboo forest(free, best before 9am when its just you and the creaking). 
 - Next door is Tenryuji temple. Worth it (500 yen) to see pond garden. 
 - Traveled across togeskyou bridge. 
 - Cheap curry lunch near station (750 yen) 
 - Early afternoon I was in Nishiki market grazing(instead of sitting down for lunch). Skewer of this, slice of tamagoyaki that. Probably 1200ish yen but enough to count as lunch/snack 
 - Kiyomizu dera in the late afternoon. Worth it to see in the light(400 yen entry). 
 - Walked down sannenzaka and ninenzaka. Free to walk around. Best looking streets imo. 
 - Katsu curry. Last dinner. 1100 yen 
 2 day/2night. Probably ~19k total. So I banked another whole day worth of budget by day 2. Its not about suffering. More about getting to places before throngs and avoiding getting you to buy expensive tea to avoid them. And about using a bike to replace half your budget in transit.

Landed in kansai on a tuesday in october. Spending ¥15,000 a day (~$100). By the time i left, i'm pretty sure Kyoto is one of the easiest places to do it. It's just taxis for bikes, and Michelin for Tofu. 
 Day 1: 
 Haikyu hostel. By kyoto station. ~¥3400 a night for dorm bed. ICOCA card. Buy it at the station kiosk. 
 Rent a bike at the hostel for ~¥800 a day instead of buses (kyoto is flat as can be and there are bike lanes everywhere). 
 - breakfast: pastry + coffee from Lawson konbini. ~¥450 
 - Bike to Fushimi Inari before 8am. Beat the tour buses. Free to enter the gates. Can walk to the yotsutsuji overlook in ~40min. 
 - Lunch: soba standing counter place near there. ~¥600 kitsune soba 
 - Tofuku ji afternoon. ¥500 to get in. for the garden. 
 - Bike to gion area, walk around. 
 Free to walk around Hanamikoji street. Free to peep into Yasaka shrine. 
 - Dinner: counter ramen place in Pontocho. ¥900 for a bowl. A can of Asahi from vending machine. ¥150. 
 Overall day 1 is ~¥10,200. So under budget. 
 Day 2: 
 Don't do hostel breakfast. Do konbini onigiri. ~¥300 
 Bike out to Arashiyama. Bamboo grove. Free. Best to do before 9am. Just you and the bamboo groan. 
 Next door is tenryuji temple. ¥500. For the pond garden. 
 Walk across togetsukyo bridge. 
 Cheap curry for lunch near the station. ~¥750. 
 Early afternoon spent grazing at nishiki market instead of a sit down meal. Here a skewer, grab some tamagoyaki. ~¥1,200 ish. Probably enough to call lunch / snack. 
 Late afternoon - Kiyomizu-dera. Beautiful light. ¥400 to get in. 
 Walk down through sannenzaka / ninenzaka. Free. Most beautiful streets in the city. 
 Dinner is like...katsu curry. ¥1,100 
 2 days / 2 nights. ~¥19,000 total. 
 So i have basically almost an extra full day's budget left over by day 2. It's not about being poor. It's about seeing temples before the crowds. (Which is also before you start to have to buy ridiculously priced tea to get away from crowds) And just replacing half your transport budget with a bike.

blog_personal_07_luna.text:
On January 1st, 2025, I deleted Facebook and Instagram on my phone. I committed to not using either for 6 months. No big post. Just told my friends and family who I’m close to, that they could just text me. 
 Initially it felt very physical. You’d wait in line at Blue Bottle in Oakland for coffee and unlock your phone, reach for the Instagram, and realize that it’s not there. Probably looked at my phone 30 times a day for no reason during the first week. By February it had definitely declined. I started bringing a paperback. Novels mostly. Plus that gardening book I’d ignored sitting on my nightstand since 2023. 
 My mind seemed much quieter. I didn’t realize how often I’d been comparing my “Tuesday” to a filtered vacation, kitchen reno or career change. The absence of all that stopped me from feeling behind (sort of) in my own life. I seemed to retain more of what I was reading/listening to. Instead of scrolling before bed, I’d read with my daughter (Maya) for 20 minutes a night. We got through 5 chapter books between January and June. 
 Would I miss big news? Friends? Maybe. I did miss a few bdays. Realized a few friendships are mostly kept alive via likes and story replies. But I also had more meaningful interactions. I spoke twice with my college friend, Daniel in Chicago (which we haven’t done in a long time). Started sending Sunday voice messages to my sister. 
 Coming back was rough. I re-installed both apps on July 1st. I thought I’d be refreshed and virtuous. Instead, I was right back to my old habits within 3 days. Deleted them again. But this time only left Facebook on laptop for certain family groups. 
 Being off for 6 months didn’t make me more productive or enlightened. It just helped me be more aware of what I’m choosing. Or what’s choosing me. I realized I’m not really missing social media that much. I’m missing people. Now I know to contact them.

On January 1st, 2025, I uninstalled Facebook and Instagram on my phone and vowed to abstain from using them for six months. I didn't really write an epic post about it. I just informed a few close friends and family that they should text me instead.

It was surprisingly physical in the beginning. I would unlock my phone when I went to get coffee at Blue Bottle in Oakland. My hand would instinctively reach for Instagram. But then I realized, "Oh no! I don't have that anymore." I'd probably check my phone 30 times a day for no real reason the first week. But in February, I was significantly less likely to check. I had a paperback book in my bag instead. I read mostly novels, but also finally read a gardening book I hadn't even touched on my nightstand since 2023.

My mind felt so much calmer overall. I didn't realize how much I had been comparing my Tuesday to someone else's elaborately curated vacation or kitchen remodel or career update. I wasn't vaguely failing my own life, because I wasn't seeing that much of it. And I found myself remembering what I read and heard more. I didn't mindlessly scroll before bed. I ended up reading for 20 minutes with my daughter Maya and we went through five chapter books in January - June.

I thought maybe I'd miss out on crucial information. I'd miss some birthdays and discovered that some friendships were largely kept up through liking their posts and responding to stories. But I found I had more conversations. I called my college friend Daniel in Chicago twice (we hadn't spoken in years) and my sister and I started sending Sunday voice memos to each other.

Coming back was the hardest part. On July 1st, I reinstalled them. I thought I'd feel all "fresher" and "disciplined." But within three days I found myself in the same bad habits again. So I uninstalled them again. This time I kept Facebook installed on my laptop just for specific family groups.

My six months sans social didn't make me more productive or enlightened. It just made me aware of what I was doing, or having done to me. It turns out that I don't really miss social media that much. I miss some people. I know who I need to contact now.

blog_personal_09_glm.text:
Baking sourdough at 5,000 ft after 30 disappointing loaves

Moved from Chicago to Boulder last June, thought I could bring my sourdough experience with me. Had two years of amazing loaves at sea level using my starter, aptly named 'Gerald' after my grandfather. Then I baked my first loaf at 5,430 ft and ended up with a hockey puck as dense as a brick and tasting of disappointment. 
 Loaf 1-8 gummy, dense middle 
 Loaf 9-15 burnt bottom, raw inside. 
 Husband Dave started to hint that we should probably just buy bread for loaf 20. 
 Hell no. I've come too far. 
  You're not going to hear this from anyone. At 5,000 ft water boils at a lower temp. (202 degrees F for me. 212 at sea level) the pressure in the air is 17% less. And the dough rises quickly and then suddenly deflates. 
 So, at sea level I was doing a bulk ferment for 4 hrs. and didn't realize it was overproofing my dough. The structure was collapsing. 
 For loaf 30, I finally call Flour bakery in Denver and desperately ask a baker, Marta, to help me over the phone. She gently laughs and makes the recommendations that made all the difference: 
 1. I reduce water by about 8%. 350g. water to 322g. for 500g. flour. Needs more structure for high altitude. 
 2. Reduce bulk ferment from 4 hrs. to 2.5 hrs. No longer relying on the clock. Looking for 50% rise rather than double. 
 3. And here's the blasphemy. I reduce my starter from 100g to 75g. to slow things down. 
 To bake, I increased temp in Dutch oven to 500 degrees F for first 20 min. with lid. Then decreased temp to 450 degrees F, uncovered for 22 min. (instead of 25). The initial heat really helps set crust before it overexpands and then falls. 
 For loaf 31, baked on a snowy Saturday this past January. Great ear to hang a picture on. The crumb was open. Glossy. Tangy, a bit. The kids (Mia 7 and Owen 4) have been politically eating my disappointments. They cheered. 
 Not so much about reducing/increasing hydration. But about forgetting. Forgetting all that I 'thought' I knew for the last 2 years, in order to adapt. Gerald and I are back to learning. Not a bad place to be. 
 If you're over 4,000 ft. and struggling with your sourdough. Your starter isn't bad. You're not bad. Make some changes. Focus on dough instead of the clock. Hang on until loaf 30.

Baking sourdough at 5000ft elevation. What 30 bad loaves taught me. 
 We left Chicago for Boulder last June. I'm sure my sourdough skills will follow with no issues. Gerald (my grandfather's name for my beloved starter) has been turning out the most beautiful loaves for 2 years at sea level. 
 I tried loaf one at 5430ft. I ended up with a hockey puck. Brick dense. Full of regret. 
 Loaves 1-8 = gummy gushy insides. Loaves 9-15 = bottom singed. Inside underdone. 
 By loaf 20 my husband Dave is politely asking if we should just buy bread. Not going to happen. I'm too far into this now. 
 They don't tell you. Water boils at a lower temp (it's 202F for us vs 212F at sea level). Air pressure is about 17% lower. Dough rises so quickly and also falls so quickly. My 4 hour bulk ferment at sea level? It's over proofing the dough. By the time I even notice, the structure can't support the bread. 
 By loaf 30 I call Flour in Denver. Ask my baker friend Marta to give me some advice on the phone. She laughs sympathetically. 
 Changes:
 * I decrease the water by about 8% (350g to 322g/500g flour). I need more structure in my high altitude dough
 * Bulk ferment instead of 4 hours go 2.5.  Stop timing. I'm looking for 50% rise not doubling
 * Sacrilege. I decrease my starter from 100g to 75g. Slow it down. 
 To bake. Increase dutch oven temp from 475F to 500F for first 20 mins (covered)  then to 450F (uncovered) for 22 mins vs 25. That higher temp burst gives me the crust before the inside over expands and collapses. 
 Last snow Saturday in January. Loaf 31. Ear = hang a picture from it. Great crumb. Luster. Slightly tangy. My kids Mia (7) and Owen (4) who had been graciously understanding my misadventures - cheer. 
 It's not really about my hydration. It's about unlearning. I've had this all figured out for 2 years. I had to deconstruct this in order to adapt. Gerald and I are learning again. And - it's not a bad place to be. 
 If you're baking over 4000ft and having trouble. Your starter isn't messed up. You're not. Adapt. Don't time it. Look at your dough. Be patient. Don't give up by loaf 30.

blog_personal_11_sonnet.text:
So, I sent out my first invoice on October 14th of last year for $340 (to write a blog post about industrial water filtration — I didn't know what that was three days ago).

And now I've sent 118 more invoices.

So, for the year. $38,240.

27 clients.

I want to write about what happened before I wrap it up in a pretty bow.

You know what blew me away?

It wasn't how much money.

It was the composition of it. $24,000 was from 4 clients.

A SaaS company called Ledgerly. $1400/month from me for a newsletter and 2 blog posts.

A dental marketing company in Ohio that pays me every week like clockwork for $600.

And then 23 other clients. Landing pages here and there. Email sequences. $75 product description for some dog leash company.

Added up to the other $14,000 and probably ate 60% of my time.

I had no idea about fixed costs vs retainer type things until I charted in July.

Error 1. I gave a fintech client a flat rate of $2,200 for 'website copy'. Without defining pages.

So now in March I'm 11 pages in. And basically making $9/hour.

I finished the project cuz I said yes.

Error 2. Didn't save any money for taxes. Didn't do this until my accountant Priya asked if I did estimated taxes in April.

I didn't.

Owed $6,100 to be paid by June 15.

Had to dip into savings.

Error 3. Held on to a client for 5 months (a supplement brand) despite the fact they started paying me 20-30 days late on their checks.

Because I liked it.

Ended up firing them in August owing me $1,900.

Never really recouped that fully.

So I guess it's not worth it to do this?

Nope.

I left a $61k salary job in Sept of last year.

So $38,240 and learning all of this stuff in 1 year while doing it for the first time from 0.

I'll take that number.

Next year?

Less clients. Better contracts.

And I'll put a kill switch on those that are late to pay after 15 days.

Not 5 months.

blog_personal_13_luna.text:
January 2025. My A1C was 8.4%. Sick of the illusion that "eating kind of good" is a solid strategy. Dr. Lena Morales at Kaiser Permanente in Sacramento said we could medicate me. However, since I was not experiencing an immediate crisis, she and I settled on a six month experiment where we would intensely monitor my diet, exercise (walks), sleep, weight reduction.

I purchased an inexpensive spiral notebook. I began logging everything. Not only what I ate. I logged times, amount eaten, feelings after meals. First day of breakfast journal. "7:30 a.m. Bagel with cream cheese. Banana. Coffee." Two hours later my glucose was 196 mg/dL. I didn't freak out, but I started to see patterns. Bread (toast), rice, cereal, large amounts of potatoes would hike numbers up fast.

In February I started making eggs with spinach, plain Greek yogurt with walnuts. Or if I had chicken & veggies leftover. I would still go eat tacos at El Rincon on Fruitridge Rd. on Fridays. But I only ordered 2 (instead of 4). No sugary horchata. After dinner, I'd go for walks around our neighborhood with my wife Marisol. 20 minutes. After a while, those walks turned into 35 minutes, 5 days a week.

Most difficult part: It wasn't perfection. It was consistency. I did have a slice of chocolate cake at my grandson Mateo's birthday (April). I logged it. Didn't throw in the towel. My notebook showed me it wasn't one dessert. But 3 weeks of quitting made all the difference.

June. My A1C was down to 7.1%. Sept. My A1C was 6.5%. I had dropped 24 lbs. since January. My most recent A1C (Jan. 10. 2026) was 6.1%. This year I have avoided taking diabetes meds. BUT only because I'm seeing them consistently. And with their approval. I still monitor my glucose. And I know things can change.

My notebooks are stacked next to my coffee maker. Yes, I have many bad days logged. But I have evidence that little decisions. (Less rice. More veggies. Go for a walk after dinner.) can make an entirely different year.

blog_personal_15_glm.text:
On March 8th, 2023. 7:45 AM Pacific time. I log into my laptop. Before I even get my coffee ready. Meta access revoked. 11 years in the industry. 4 years as a technical program manager on Reality Labs team. Ended by a calendar invite called 'Important Update' that I didn't get to attend.

90 days later. Writing from a coffee shop in Austin. Just signed an offer for a new role. Here's my sanity saving recovery plan.

Days 1-14 - Be intentionally sad. 

Take 2 solid weeks of bad feelings. Get severance paperwork done (16 weeks + prorated feb bonus. First weekend running all numbers so no money panic surprises) Uninstall Slack from your phone. Block all the ex-colleagues celebration posts. Walk around Lady Bird lake at the time you used to be logging in every morning. Scaffolding is the thing.

Days 15-45 - Fix the scaffolding 

Updated LinkedIn on Mar20. Expected the pity. Instead notifications went nuts. Received 11 messages from ex-colleagues in a week. 6 of which were also laid off. Started a discord channel 'Laid off and loaded with caffeine'. Meet virtually every Tuesday. Got referrals from this group. Not cold applications.

Applied to exactly 40 jobs.

That's all. Quality over quantity. Every application had a customised resume. Went after a warm intro for 30 of them.

Days 46-90. Interview like it's your job (because it is) 

Mock interview 2x week. 1x with my friend Priya. 1x recorded on Loom for you to cringe about your filler words. Failed a system design for a fintech in April. Allowed myself 1 evening to mope around. Then 3 pages of notes on what went wrong.

New offer (which I signed yesterday) is a program management role with a healthcare startup. 15% less base comp than Meta. But maybe meaningful equity. 

I'm sleeping better. My old team had projects under constant reorg. This company has a stable roadmap since Jan. No pivots. 

If you received that calendar invite in March. Here's my game plan in one sentence. Allow yourself to be sad. Don't apply too much. Let your network save you when you cannot walk.

90 days is doable. You're more than your badge access.

It's March 8, 2023. 7:45am pacific. I open up my laptop before I finish getting my coffee. My access is already gone from Meta. After 11 years in tech. 4 of those years as a technical program manager at the Reality Labs team. It all came down to a calendar invite for an "Important Update" that I didn't actually get to see. 
 Now exactly 90 days later I'm in a coffee shop in Austin. Just accepted an offer for a new job. And here's the recovery plan that kept me sane: 
  0-14: Cry on purpose. Take two full weeks to feel like shit. Get your severance in order (16 weeks. Feb bonus prorated. First weekend I went through all the math so I wouldn't get blindsided by money stress later). Ditch slack on your phone. Block everyone happy for your ex-coworkers. Every morning, walk around lady bird lake at the same time you used to "come in." Scaffolding is important. 
  15-45: Build the scaffolding back up. March 20th, I updated my linkedin.  Prepare to get hit with pity. 
 Haha nope! I got bombarded with notifications! 11 ex-colleagues hit me up in the first week! 6 of them got laid off too! We created a discord: "Laid Off and loaded on Caffeine." We met up virtually every Tuesday. I was getting referrals from this group. No cold applications. 
 40 jobs. That's all. Applied to 40 jobs.  Quality over quantity. Personalized resume for all of them. For 30 of them, I pursued a warm intro. 
 46-90: "It's your job to interview. Because it is your job." - 2 mock interviews a week.  1 with my friend Priya. 1 recorded on loom so I could cringe at my own "ums" and "ahs" 
  System design round at a fintech in April. 
 Fucked it up. 
 Gave myself one night to mope. 
 But then 3 pages of notes on how it failed. 
 The new job I accepted yesterday is a program management role in a healthcare startup. 15% less base than Meta. But.. some equity that could matter? And tbh I sleep better. Projects on my previous team were always in flux. Getting reorganized.  This place has a roadmap that hasn't shifted since January. 
 If you got that calendar invite in March. Here's the TLDR of my plan.  1. Grieve in a controlled way. 2. Ration applications.  3. Your network will lift you up when your feet fail. 
 90 days. We can do this. 
 You are not your access badge.

essay_opinion_00_glm.text:
I started instagram in october 2013. when you could just post squares. i cared so much about filters. it was mostly clarendon. last month on a tuesday evening in march, i deleted instagram after 11 years. after 14,000 photos/stories/likes.

it wasn't a dramatic scene. no scandal. no 数据 breach. no public declaration. in the end the straw that broke the camel's instagram back was embarrassingly small. i realized i was watching a random person renovate a campervan in portugal in a reel while my 6 year old was talking about a drawing she made for me. 'uh-huh' (x4). not really listening. she stopped talking in the middle. that sting. worse than any screen time report.

i've tried moderating it before. grayscale mode. app timers. the digital minimalism craze. it wasn't the amount of time per se. though, per my iphones screen time settings its 2+ hours a day. not insignificant. but it was more that instagram had shaped my attention. i thought about meals and sunsets and my backyard as pre-content. i once rearranged my pasta plate in my aunt's yonkers house. for better lighting. she still mentions it.

what surprised me the most was that the habit was actually mostly about idle hands and threshold moments. not about craving. but about wake up time. about waiting for your coffee. about being in line at the bodega.

so i substituted. not the app. but the slot for it. kindle in my pocket instead of my phone. i've read 9 books since march. vs 3 in all of last year. my paper notebook when i want to check something (anything) in the bathroom line. walking the wrong and slow way to the subway. not on the platform. scrolling.

i won't say that everything changed. there were 3 ugly days of phantom thumb swiping on the home screen for the now non-existent app. there are half my acquaintances i don't know what they're doing. that sometimes stings. i missed a friends engagement announcement. i had to actually use words to apologize.

but here's the surprise. i got bored again. real fruitful boredom. you know? when you realize you've had the broken chair wobbly for 2 years. so you fix it. then you just sit there. quiet. and don't take a photo for anyone.

if you're considering, you don't need to have a better reason than wanting your own attention back. i was waiting 11 years for a good enough reason. 'just wanted to' turns out was good enough.

I signed up in October 2013, when you could only post square photos, when the biggest question I had was what filter to use (it was usually Clarendon). And then, last month, on a Tuesday night in March, after 11 years and around 14k posts, stories, likes, etc., I deleted Instagram.

No big scandal. No data breach. No public whumping manifesto. The straw that broke this particular camel was an embarrassingly trivial one: The other day, I noticed myself staring in rapt attention at this reel of some random person converting a camper van in Portugal, while my six-year-old was describing, out loud, this drawing she had done for me...and I was saying 'uh-huh' four times over without even registering a single syllable. Mid-sentence, she paused. It was a worse pause than any screen-time report.

I'd already attempted to moderate my usage: grayscale, app time limits, all the cottage industry of digital minimalism. It wasn't really a matter of minutes (though 2+ hrs a day according to my iphone screen time settings was not nothing). It was that IG had shaped the very structure of my attention. I was eating meals, and watching sunsets, and observing my own garden as 'pre-content'. I've even rearranged pasta on a plate at my aunt's house in Yonkers once for better light. She won't let me forget it.

What I didn't realize was the true content of this habit. It wasn't really lustful. It was about spare moments, and about thresholds: when I'm waking up; when I'm waiting for coffee; when I'm in line at the bodega. So, I filled in the slots. But with other things than IG. Like a kindle in my pocket instead of my phone (I've read 9 books since March, vs 3 all last year). Paper notebook to deal with the 'check it, goddammit, check it' while in bathroom line impulse. Walking (slowly and poorly) towards the subway, instead of standing on the platform scrolling.

Did everything change? Not entirely. For three 'ugly' days, I was still doing that phantom thumb swipe on the home screen in search of a deleted IG. I still don't know what half my acquaintances are doing. And sometimes, it hurts. Like, I missed my friend's engagement announcement and I had to apologize, with my words.

But, here's the unexpected thing: boredom returned. Rich, fertile boredom where you start to realize you wanted to fix that wobbly chair for the past 2 years. I fixed it. Then sat with quiet. Didn't take a photo of it. To share.

If you're considering it, there's no better reason than 'wanting my own attention back'. 11 years I waited for some good enough reason. Turns out, 'just because I wanted to', was enough.

essay_opinion_02_sonnet.text:
Quit my RTO job at fintech in Charlotte (March 2024). Everyone thought it was the commute.  No.  It was 11am 'quick sync' that lasted 90min because our VP needed to talk his way through his thought process before making a decision for 11 people (4 had no bearing on the decision). 
 
 People keep waging this battle over remote work in the wrong arena.  Execs. will pull badge swipes and claim that collaboration has suffered.  Employees. will whine about their commute and insist that 2h per day is their deal breaker.  Both sides keep arguing over location but it's the SCHEDULE that's the disease.  Dropbox discovered (2023) that their employees averaged 21 hours/week in meetings.  The Anatomy of Work report by Asana has been saying for 3 years straight that people consider more than half their meetings a waste of time.  It wasn't a 2020 thing.  Zoom didn't create the 'should have been an email' meeting.  It just had a gallery view. 
 
 I've been in offices where they managed meetings well.  A startup in Austin.  Perhaps 40 people.  The CEO made a rule that if there was no written agenda for a meeting, it got cancelled by his assistant and there was no recourse.  People wanted to be there.  No one was wanting to 'make up' their commute.  It was valuable to be inside.  In contrast, the Charlotte job that I had, calendar was this puzzle of recurring standups that no one seemed to remember signing up for.  Office was ok.  Good coffee.  Nice espresso machine.  Natural light on 9th floor.  Building wasn't it.  45min of my day staring at someone reading off a slide was it. 
 
 RTO orders are making a bet that being near each other will create value.  It keeps losing because it's not taking the right variable.  Salesforce, Amazon, Dell, etc have been pushing hard for the 5 day week again over the last two years.  Still those internal surveys are showing that meeting fatigue is the number 1 complaint.  Not 'hating' commute.  You can force them back into the building and they'll just have their terrible meetings in the flesh instead of the screen.  Same rot.  Suckier parking. 
 
 If companies want to matter offices again, they need to start by slashing their recurring meetings in half.  Not their remote days in half.

 We always argue the wrong thing on the remote work discussion. Execs talk about how many badge swipes they have and say it's because there's less collaboration. Employees say how much they commute and say 2 hours a day is a no-go. Everyone's arguing about location when what's causing the problem is scheduling. For 3 years in a row, Asana's 'anatomy of work' report says people think >50% of meetings are a waste of time. It's not a 2020 problem. Zoom didn't create the meeting should-be-an-email problem. They just added a gallery. 
 There are offices I've worked in where the meeting culture was on point. For example, I worked in a startup in Austin with ~40 people. The CEO made it a policy that if you didn't have a written agenda, his assistant would cancel the meeting and there's no appealing. People loved going to that office. There was no trying to squeeze more commute time back. The time you spent in that office mattered. But then there was my job in charlotte where the calendar was like a tetris board of forgotten recurring stand-up meetings. The office itself was fine. Great coffee. Nice espresso machine. Natural light on the 9th floor. The office itself wasn't the problem. It was the 45 minutes of my day where I had to sit there and watch someone present a slide via read-aloud. 
 You're making an rto mandate and saying it's because we think you'll create value if you just put people in the same place. essay_opinion_04_luna.text:
Lesson 1 about digital nomads from Lisbon's housing crisis: Living anywhere pretty much means taking up space that other people can no longer afford.

October 2022. Suitcase. The usual pitch: online work, paid in dollars, let's live here, slow down. $1,600-a-month apartment in Arroios. That's more than a lot of local salaries, but bargain! Only 3-month lease. Used to be an Airbnb for tourists. (Landlord rented to tourists before.)

Cafes in Intendente / Graça. Chat with other remote workers. Compare neighborhoods and wifi. Discuss visas. All very excited about "community." But not much mention of who's lost the community in the process. A bartender tells me that she and her partner moved to Setúbal after they got a €300 rent hike. Now it takes her nearly 2 hours one way to get to central Lisbon. She's not after a lifestyle. She's after a home.

The awkward truth is that digital nomadism is geography arbitrage. We're taking salaries from richer economies and entering spaces with already-stressed housing markets. On an individual level, we might be nice and interested and good at sorting recyclables. But on a collective level, we're still able to make a neighborhood less habitable for those who made it.

Lisbon hasn't taught me that foreigners are the special source of its housing crisis. There's a lot more to it: years of speculation, short-term rentals, weak renters' rights, low wages, and so on. No one group of newcomers is the most important. But we're part of the demand. And we're so good at using language to obscure this. We say we're "flexible," when really we're just flush with cash.

These days, every time I hear someone talk about the freedom of being able to work from anywhere, I remember that bartender's commute. "Anywhere" is not a blank canvas. It's got schools and grandparents and rent-controlled apartments. And people who don't have a return ticket.

The most non-digital-nomad-like thing I can imagine doing is to ask myself: Sure. Can I afford to live here? But what's going to happen to this place if we, a bunch of us like this, find out that we can?

What I learned from Lisbon's housing crisis: the first lesson about digital nomads is that when you're "living anywhere", you're often living where other people can't afford it anymore.

I landed in Lisbon in October 2022 with a suitcase and the usual pitch. I work online, in dollars. I want to take my time and see what this city has to offer. I had a place in Arroios. €1150 per month. A lot for many people here. A deal, though, because it was a 3 month lease. Before, it was rented to tourists on Airbnb.

In the cafes near Intendente or Graça, I'd meet other remote workers. We'd swap notes on neighborhoods and Wifi and visas. We talked a lot about "community". But we didn't talk as much about the people who were displaced from that community. A bartender said she and her boyfriend moved to Setubal. Their rent had gone up €300. Her trip to the center of Lisbon was almost 2 hours round-trip. She wasn't looking for a lifestyle. She was looking for a home.

It's an uncomfortable truth, but the thing about digital nomads is that we're arbitrageing geography. We're taking our wages, earned in wealthier places, to places with housing strains. As individuals, we can be nice and thoughtful and use our recycling bins. But as a group, we can still make a neighborhood un-livable for the people who made it that way.

I didn't learn from Lisbon that it's just foreigners that are the problem. It's not just foreigners that caused their housing crunch. It's years of speculation, short-term lets, a lack of renter's rights, and low wages. More than anything. But we're a demand. And we're often too clever to admit it. We say we're flexible, but really we're just rich.

Now, when I hear someone extolling the virtues of working from anywhere, I think about the bartender's commute. It's not just a blank canvas for "anywhere". It's a place with schools and grandparents and rent-controlled flats. It's a place for people that don't have a return ticket.

The least digital-nomad-like thing I can think of would be to not just ask "Can I afford to live here?" but "What does this place look like if thousands of people like me decide they can?"

The first thing I do upon arriving Haneda Airport at 1am a Tuesday in March is go to 7-Eleven.

Onigiri. Salmon, ¥140. Sealed in plastic that keeps the nori fresh up until you open it, patented in the 70s and since then improved. Until now.

I'm eating it on the street, Meguro. Standing up. Dazed. Jet-lagged.

Fuck. That's the best fucking rice ball I've ever eaten.

This is what they're like, the convenience stores in Tokyo. The konbini. There are over 56,000 of them in Japan. In Tokyo alone, over 7,000. So you're never more than a couple hundred metres from a 7-11. Or any other.

Yes, it's a joke, this is what it's like to be alone in the modern world, the glowing sad lights of pre-packaged food that never turns off. But I've lived in Nakano for three years now. And I've come to realize the konbini is one of the most brilliant and sophisticated pieces of urban design you can imagine.

Think of the logistics.

They re-stock the store three times a day. Because the bento is fresh. Prepared that day. And sold off cheaper in the evening. It knows what's going to sell and what's not. Shogayaki pork for lunch, for example, will sell in Shinjuku but not Setagaya. The supply is tailored to each store accordingly. And it's not sitting on the shelf.

The food is great. Good stuff. The Karaage. The egg sandwiches. The oden in the pot at the checkout in the winter. It's more than once cost me more for worse food in New York.

But the magic of the konbini is more than that.

So you can pay your electricity bill. You can print out stuff. Buy concert tickets. Send luggage. Get cash out. (They take international cards. Which was a lifesaver.)

Tokyo restaurants were closing early in the pandemic. The konbini took the hours of eating in Tokyo in stride.

The government started charging for plastic bags in 2019. The konbini rolled over night.

But what fascinates me the most is the social aspect.

The old man who stops by every morning at 6:40 for his cup of coffee and Sankei Shimbun. It's not just a cup of coffee for breakfast. He's saying hi. The store clerk knows him. It's Tokyo. 37 million people. This is the corner store. But it's Tokyo's corner store. Magnified with frightening accuracy. But somehow still personal.

What is it that we in the West are always looking for? How do we make the city more livable? Walkable? Human?

Maybe it's standing on the corner of Koenji Dori at 3am and fully lit. Hot coffee. Fried chicken. Umbrellas. Just asking you for 130¥.

I arrive Haneda airport at 1am on a Tuesday in March. The first thing I do is go into a 7-11 and grab an onigiri. Salmon. 140 yen. In plastic that's been perfectly engineered so the seaweed remains crispy until the last second before you open it. A design that's been patented in the 1970s and improved on for decades. I eat it on the sidewalk in Meguro while jetlagged and a bit loopy. And I think to myself: this is the best rice ball I've ever had.

That's what it's like with the convenience stores in Tokyo. They're called konbini. There are 56k+ in all of Japan. In Tokyo there are 7,000+. So they're never really far away. Often just a few hundred meters. We make fun of them in a way as a symptom of our modern alienation. The lonely bright beacon of processed food burning through the night. But I've lived in Nakano for 3 years now. And I've realised the konbini might be one of the most sophisticated bits of infrastructure in the world.

You take the logistical side. For example the store is typically restocked 3 times a day because the bento's for that day are made in the morning. That evening they'll discount it. They know that in Shinjuku people are going to buy shogayaki pork for lunch. Not in setagaya. And they adjust the supply for each store accordingly. There's never any waste. The food's actually pretty good. Like the karaage. The egg sandwiches. The Oden on the counter by the cash register in winter. I've had worse meals at 3x the price in NYC.

We had a 4-day week trial last October. Well, it was four days in trial for four months. We started it largely because our operations manager, Priya, kept emailing us article after article about it. 
 We're a 22-person logistics software company in Leeds and were losing people. 3 resignations that summer. So, on some rainy grey Tuesday we had the directors say "we're going to shut the office on a Friday for 6 months and see how it goes". 
 I was thinking "shitshow". Instead, it was a death of a performative meeting. 
 What they don't tell you about 4-day week. 
 The 5th day wasn't the thing. It's the 'realisation' of all the performative stuff we were doing on the 4 days. The status meeting on Monday that goes 90 mins? Now it's 25 mins. Suddenly they all have places to be. Their life. 
 All those 'quick sync's' that aren't quick and are really someone avoiding a decision in writing? Well, no more. By November the team chat has an unwritten rule "if you can message, message". 
 Oh, and we saw 14% decrease in ticket response time to customer. It wasn't from people doing more. It's Tom finally getting some time to re-write the ticket routing system. The 'I meant to get round to that for 2 years'. That Friday meant he can get headspace to do that. Only we didn't do it on Friday's. We did it by creating the headspace of 'Friday exists'. We don't feel bad. 
 It was more the cultural shift. And it came gradually. Like re-arrangement of furniture. Suddenly people would say when they were blocked. I think it's the 4 day week implicitly said "your time is precious. We won't waste your time". And that made wasting your own time seem more silly. Our junior dev, Marcus, asked for help with a problem in week 2. He said later he'd normally have held off a month with it. 
 Not all worked. Some clients initially did not like not having a Friday contact. We switched the support rotations. One colleague, Dillon, still worked from home on Friday's out of habit. It took a chat to get him to understand. It's not about getting 5 days of work in 4. 
 After the trial ended in April. 21-1 to continue. (Dillon said yes). 
 I don't think about 4-day week in terms of scheduling. It's about honesty. If you make a week shorter, you make the excuses shorter. Turns out our collaboration was mostly mutual avoidance. With a calendar invite.

 That 'Friday' gave people headspace to do things like that. We just didn't use Fridays. 
 We used the headspace created from the guilt-free feeling of having the 'Friday'

last tuesday. 8:47pm. order milk. bananas. a sack of rice. from quickcart - the 15 minute grocery delivery app. 8:59pm - the rider (blue helmet) drops your order on the sidewalk in front of your valencia st. apartment building. 'magic,' you think. until you see him, legs running back to his electric bike. eyes on the next notification.

in my neighborhood the 15 minutes has become a new tempo. ever since quickcart and dashbasket moved in with their dark-grocery warehouses in 2024 there are idle delivery people around the corner store. bikes in the way of the curb-cuts. bus stops. riding in rain. heat. in the hushed, dark hours of the night. paid per delivery. docked (several riders i've talked to) for late deliveries. how we define fast for ourselves is often just someone else's stressed out.

there's a human cost to thinking of a carton of eggs as an emergency. the riders dart through valencia traffic. 24th st. trying to beat the app timer. you've seen them hop the curb to bypass a double-parked van. or stand outside waiting in the dark of a december night. because apartment buildings have locked lobbies. i spoke to a rider who made $118 (before expenses) for a ten hour shift last saturday. not even enough to buy one of those battery's for a delivery scooter, let alone sf rent.

then there's a neighborhood cost. the old corner markets who knew their customers now pitted against the vc-millions-backed go-tos for those impulse purchases. no cafe. no bulletin board. no old person asking about your family. just these efficient, faceless boxes tuned to channel the hunger, absent-minded, boredom into something that can be bought.

i still use them. sometimes my disabled neighbor wants groceries. or i need meds. realize i'm out at 9pm. no chance to leave work. but i'm trying to tell myself the truth about 'instant.' it's not making food happen any faster. it's making someone else bear the inconvenience. on a bike. in traffic. with a wage not quite covering living in the city. so your groceries might get there in 15 mins. but the bill, as always, is due later.

Last Tuesday, at 8:47 pm, I ordered milk, bananas, and a bag of rice from QuickCart: 15 min grocery. By 8:59, a rider with a blue helmet dropped my order outside my apartment on Valencia St. It seemed magical. Until I saw the guy sprinting back to his electric bike, looking at his next notification.

Here, fifteen minutes is remaking the city's streets. Since 2024, when QuickCart and DashBasket opened their dark grocery warehouses in my neighborhood, delivery riders are parked next to every corner market—obstructing the curb cuts and bus stops. They deliver through rain and heat and the dead of night. They're paid by the delivery, and—from what I've heard from multiple riders—get dinged for late deliveries. Convenience, for us, is often just someone else's stress.

There's a human price to the idea that a carton of eggs is urgent. Riders are speeding down Valencia and 24th St, dodging cars, against the app's timer. I've seen them climb onto the sidewalk to dodge a double-parked van. Or sit outside, in the darkness of December, when apartment building lobbies are locked. Last Saturday, I heard one rider earned $118 in a 10-hour shift, before expenses. That's not even enough to buy a single battery for a delivery scooter, much less live in San Francisco.

And then there's the price to the neighborhood. Little markets that once knew their customers now have to compete with the VC-backed (millions) companies that cater to spur-of-the-moment buying. No café. No bulletin board. No old person to ask about your family. Just efficient, faceless rooms where hunger, or forgetfulness, or boredom gets converted into transactions.

I use it. Sometimes my disabled neighbor needs groceries. Sometimes at 9pm I remember I'm out of medicine and can't get away from work. But I'm trying to be clear about what 'instant' means. It doesn't mean food comes faster. It means someone else is getting to deal with the hassle—on a bike, in traffic, for a wage that can't even keep them in this city. We get our groceries in 15 mins. As always, we'll pay the price later.

When President Truman signed the European Recovery Program (what most know as the Marshall Plan) into law on April 3, 1948, the economic prospects for West Germany were grim: not only were the industrial cities devastated, but the currency was practically worthless, and the Allied policies limiting the economy- setting limits on the production of steel and breaking down industries - were still in place. However, during the next four years over $1.4 billion was directed to the soon-to-be Federal Republic of Germany in Marshall Plan aid, helping to spark what would become a truly astonishing economic recovery in the twentieth century.

The Marshall Plan aid, channeled through the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), was significant not so much in the sheer amount of aid but in the timing and role. Goods (such as cotton, wheat, coal, machinery) were shipped to West Germany, in exchange for Reichsmarks (which were almost worthless) which were then placed in a special counterpart fund. The several billion Deutschmarks in this fund would later be used to finance infrastructural and industrial projects - including modernization of the electrical grid and the development of the steel industry in the Ruhr Valley. Probably more importantly, the Marshall Plan aid in 1949 and 1950 helped pay for Germany's persistent trade deficit, allowing the young state of West Germany the time it needed for its currency reform (the introduction of the Deutschmark) in June 1948 to take effect.

The Marshall Plan compelled certain institutional changes which played a critical role. One, in order to accept American aid, West Germany had to become a member of the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC), and thus West Germany was integrated into a framework of European cooperation which would lead decades later to the establishment of the European Coal and Steel Community of 1951. Also, the Americans helped reduce the occupation restrictions: the ceiling on the steel production, for example, was gradually increased from about 5.8 million tons to over 11 million tons by the early 1950s. Likewise, the plant break down was mostly discontinued. Together with the social market economy policy he had initiated (combining free competition in the market with social security) - the new Economic Director, Ludwig Erhard, appointed in 1948 - took advantage of this new leeway.

The results were astounding. West Germany's industrial production increased by roughly double in the years between 1948 and 1952, and by the mid-1950s they were producing more than they had pre-war - what the government of Chancellor Konrad Adenauer hailed as the "economic miracle" (or Wirtschaftswunder). Of course, as historians wisely point out, the Marshall Plan was only one factor in the equation - currency reform, demand from the Korean War, skilled workers, etc. - were the other important factors. Nevertheless, it can be argued that the American aid not only restored the West German economy, it reshaped it - to Europe, to trade, to the stable democratic capitalism that would characterize the Federal Republic for decades to come.

On April 3, 1948, President Truman signed the law to create the European Recovery Program, known popularly as the Marshall Plan. The economic prospects for West Germany in the immediate postwar period were not very hopeful. The country's industrial areas were devastated, its currency was nearly worthless, and economic restrictions of Allied occupation policies had limited steel production and broken up industrial facilities. Nevertheless, from the Marshall Plan came about $1.4 billion for the future Federal Republic of Germany over four years, a powerful force in catalyzing one of the great economic recoveries of the twentieth century.

Not the amount, but the timing and role of Marshall Plan aid (channeled through the Economic Cooperation Administration, or ECA) were key. The ECA sent goods (cotton, wheat, coal, machinery, etc.) to West Germany. The payments for the goods were made in virtually valueless Reichsmarks, and the proceeds were placed in a special counterpart fund. The several billion Deutschmarks in this fund were then used to invest in industry and infrastructure. Infrastructure and industrial development included, for example, improving electrical grids and developing the Ruhr Valley's steel-making industry further. Arguably no less important was the Marshall Plan's role in funding Germany's large trade deficit in 1949 and 1950. It gave the new German West State some time to get the benefits of its June 1948 currency reform (the creation of the Deutschmark).

Marshall Plan aid also imposed important institutional changes. To get Marshall Plan aid, the recipients had to join the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC). This brought West Germany into a process that would eventually lead to the European Coal and Steel Community, formed in 1951. With U.S. prompting, Germany's occupation restrictions eased. Restrictions on steel production gradually grew from levels of approximately 5.8 million tons to levels of over 11 million tons by the early 1950s. Dismantling of factories also pretty much ended. Appointed Economic Director in 1948, Ludwig Erhard combined these changes with his "social market economy" economic policy: a combination of free market competition and social safety nets.

West Germany's industrial output grew nearly twice as much from 1948 to 1952 as before. By the mid-1950s, West Germany produced more than it did before the war. The Chancellor Konrad Adenauer government made much of this "economic miracle" (Wirtschaftswunder). While historians rightly point out that the Marshall Plan was only one of several factors at work (including currency reform, the needs of Korea, the war, and the skilled work force), it can be said that U.S. economic aid did more than just help recover West Germany's economy. It redirected it. Toward Europe. Toward trade. Toward the kind of stable democratic capitalist economy that characterized the Federal Republic for decades.

While the idea behind tipping is to reward good service, expecting a full 20% for "excellent" services is ethically suspect. In most US states, tipped employees are allowed by law to have sub-minimum wages ($2.13 federal minimum wage, higher wages like $9.54 (NY) and $12.00 (WA state) depend on state legislatures)  and if a server is getting paid their base pay assuming a 20% tip is going to be the baseline (not a bonus), the issue of only paying for "excellence" is moving the risk of labor costs to the restaurant from the perspective of whether the server's food was enjoyed by the guest at table 14. For a Olive Garden or small diner in Columbus Ohio it is important that they make sure their employees make enough even if it takes 9 minutes or 14 minutes for table 14 to get their entree. 
 Now I understand the counterpoint that tipping is supposed to signal something in a market context. If the full 20% is guaranteed without any "work" for the server then they will not be incentivized to put in the effort during a Friday night dinner rush. If a customer at a $40 per head restaurant is just going to give the server a flat $8 tip regardless of if they disappear for 20 minutes or if they refill your water without being asked, they are not signaling a reward for quality. They are just paying a tax. Economists like Ofer Azar who has done extensive research into tipping norms talk about how tipping can only work as an incentive if it's variable in terms of service quality (which a 20% for anything approach sort of torpedoes). 
 So a more reasonable approach is to acknowledge that there should be something like a 15% (give or take) as the ethical minimum (to make up for the sub-minimum wage thing) and that 20-25% should be reserved for exceeding service quality expectations. If someone isn't even doing as bad as below 15%, but just average, then they should be tipped below 15% only if they are negligent. It's not necessarily the variable tipping that is unethical. It's using "only if it's excellent" as an excuse to tip below what is the wage supplement to make up for the base wage (eg. for adequately sufficient service) or for just not tipping at all because of some kitchen delay that wasn't the servers fault. For that Chili's in Tampa on a Tuesday night you owe your iced tea refill person a living wage before they can even "earn" any more. (exceeding quality should be the ceiling for rewards, not the baseline for the floor).

The argument for tipping is that it incentivizes good service. But "excellent" service to deserve 100% of 20% is pretty unethical. Most places in the US are allowed to pay subminimum wages to tipped workers (2.13$ federal minimum, and $9.54 in NYC or $12.00 in Washington state are only by state legislature) so if you pay a server a wage that in base will expect 20% tip, and not just a bonus, making the 20% a "only when excellent" game makes the labor costs for your business dependent on one customer's enjoyment of their meal. If your place is an olive garden or local diner in Columbus, OH, you still have to pay them enough to live off, regardless of if they delivered table 14's entree in 9 or 14 minutes. 
 The response is also very valid. Tipping should be a market signal and if it becomes "anything = 20%" always, there's no incentive for the server to hustle the Friday dinner shift. The guy eating at a 40$ per person place who tips $8 no matter if their waiter's gone for 20 minutes or is extra responsive to water refills without prompting, isn't rewarding for quality, he's taxing you. The economics of it like Ofer Azar who has done a lot of work on the norms around tipping, and it's only a mechanism for incentive if it can actually fluctuate based on service, which is what's hurt by having this rigid 20% is always thing. 
 The more ethical approach would be that 15% or so should be the ethical minimum to serve the server's income (the sub-min wage thing), and let 20-25% be reserved for extra exceptional service but below 15% only for egregious negligence and not just "good, but not really special" service. It's not unethical to give variable tips, it's being unethical and saying "only when excellent" to justify giving tips below your wage supplement floor (your minimum) for perfectly acceptable service, or not tipping the server at all because the kitchen isn't up to par on your control. Someone eating Chili's on a Tuesday night in Tampa owes the person refilling their iced tea a living wage before they've earned extra for being exceptional. Let the ceiling be lifted by excellence, not lower the floor requirement.

essay_student_04_luna.text: In Pride and Prejudice (1813), Jane Austen points out the unfair economic situation faced by women because of inheritance law. The Bennet family lives on a property, Longbourn in Hertfordshire. It is "entailed" on the male line, which means that when Mr. Bennet dies, the property cannot be inherited by his five daughters, Jane, Elizabeth, Mary, Kitty, and Lydia. On December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to yield her seat on a city bus to a white man. This seemingly small act of civil disobedience would go on to revolutionize the civil rights movement in the United States. Rosa Parks was not just a weary seamstress as the myth has painted her to be. Rather, she was a trained activist and secretary of the Montgomery chapter of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) who consciously chose to do what she did that night, fully aware of what the outcome might be. Although Rosa Parks was arrested and fined according to Montgomery segregationist laws, her arrest would trigger events that no one could have anticipated.

In the days following her arrest, civil rights activists like Jo Ann Robinson of the Women's Political Council, distributed some 35,000 leaflets throughout the community, calling for a one day bus boycott to take place on December 5, 1955. The bus boycott was so effective that a new organization, the Montgomery Improvement Association, was organized to keep the effort going, with young pastor, 26-year-old Martin Luther King Jr., being elected as the president of the organization. The bus boycott that began as a protest against segregated bus practices quickly became a 381-day movement that saw around 40,000 Black people in the Montgomery community walking, carpooling, enduring harassment and violence to avoid the segregated bus system. Martin Luther King Jr. had his house bombed and many of the boycott participants lost their jobs or were arrested. But the community persevered.

On December 20, 1956, the Montgomery bus boycott came to an end when the Supreme Court affirmed a lower court's decision in Browder v. Gayle that segregation on the buses was unconstitutional. The successful boycott showed that large-scale nonviolent mass action could be used to overcome institutional discrimination. This victory made Martin Luther King Jr. a national figure, and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference was established in 1957.

The Montgomery Bus Boycott is important not just because it secured an important legal victory. It also set the example for the kind of activism that would shape the next decade of civil rights. It proved that people from all walks of life, such as house workers, teachers, students, and others could come together to resist an unjust system with disciplined mass action. Although Rosa Parks was the catalyst with her courageous act of defiance, it was the determination of the Black community in Montgomery that was the burning fire. Rosa Parks would later say that "the only tired I was, was tired of giving in." Her arrest and the movement that followed showed that one small act of defiance in the face of injustice could be all that is needed to resist.

In June of 2013, a then 29 year-old Booz Allen Hamilton contractor at the National Security Agency’s Hawaii installation, Edward Snowden, released to journalists Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras thousands of documents about various secret programs, such as the PRISM program and the massive collection of American phone records through Section 215 of the Patriot Act. The revelation, initially published by The Guardian on June 6th, 2013, has not only ignited a worldwide discussion about surveillance, privacy and the proper scope of state secrecy, it has also raised the more difficult question: is it ever acceptable to violate an oath and the law by breaking a sworn oath to reveal misconduct?

Snowden’s defense can be made on the grounds of consequentialism and conscience. Snowden blew the lid off of the NSA’s practice of collecting metadata from millions of Americans without individualized suspicion. A federal judge later that year, Richard Leon, has called this “almost Orwellian”. There are good reasons why whistleblowing is necessary: internal mechanisms are not always adequate. As Snowden himself has stated, he tried to complain to his co-workers, but thought his formal complaints would be covered up and used against him. Snowden’s action could be justified in utilitarian ethics - the consequences of the revelation were outweighed by the good that would result from public accountability, discussion and reform (such as the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015, which ended the mass collection of phone records).

On the other hand, Snowden’s actions are far from innocent. He broke the Espionage Act of 1917. He swore an oath to keep classified information secure. He ended up in Hong Kong, and since 2013 has resided in Moscow. So was his behavior purely principled, or self-interested? Deontologists argue that we have an important obligation to follow rules and keep promises. If an intelligence official is free to unilaterally decide what secrets the public has the right to know, we set a dangerous precedent that could cost lives or cripple legitimate security activities. Critics (such as former NSA Director Michael Hayden) argued Snowden had other legal options (such as the Intelligence Community Whistleblower Protection Act) - even if these were not perfect.

There is no easy answer to this dilemma, as it sets two important goods against each other - the rule of law and confidence in the institutions vs. the public’s right to know when the government abuses it’s own secrets. The Snowden affair indicates whistleblowing is only acceptable under limited circumstances: if the misconduct is widespread, the harm is serious and all internal avenues have been pursued. By this standard, Snowden’s action doesn’t seem like treason or heroic behavior so much as a deliberate risk-taking behavior, gambling with the knowledge that he would have to suffer consequences for revealing the truth.

In June of 2013, 29 year old NSA contractor and Booz Allen Hamilton employee Edward Snowden disclosed to journalists Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras thousands of documents containing classified information about programs such as PRISM and the mass collection of American phone records under Section 215 of the Patriot Act. When the information was published by The Guardian on June 6, 2013, it sparked a worldwide conversation about surveillance and privacy. It also raised the question of the limits of state secrecy, and perhaps more importantly, when is it justifiable to break a sworn oath and the law in the name of revealing wrong-doing?

On the one hand, there are strong arguments in favor of Snowden and his actions. At the time, he exposed the fact that the NSA was collecting metadata on millions of Americans without individualized suspicion. In 2013, federal judge Richard Leon would call the program "almost Orwellian." The importance of whistle-blowing comes from the fact that internal mechanisms of complaint are often ineffective. Snowden has claimed to have voiced his concerns to co-workers and thought formal complaints would be ignored or used against him. One could ethically justify his actions through a utilitarian lens. The negatives of blowing his whistle were outweighed by the positive effects that the public exposure would have with transparency, dialogue, and ultimately reform that would follow. This included the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015 which ended the bulk phone record collection program.

However, on the other hand, there are significant objections to Snowden's actions. Snowden broke the 1917 Espionage Act. He swore to protect classified information. He escaped first to Hong Kong and ultimately to Moscow (since 2013) where he still resides. This raises the question of the extent to which Snowden's actions were principled versus self-preservation. Deontologists would point out the moral value of rules and promises. When an intelligence officer unilaterally determines which secrets the public has the right to know, a dangerous precedent is established. This could lead to lives being put at risk or hamstring legitimate security efforts. Some opponents of Snowden (including former NSA director Michael Hayden) argued that he had legal options (although not perfect) available to him, such as the Intelligence Community Whistleblower Protection Act.

One of the problems with this particular dilemma is that it presents a situation where two good things are in tension. We have the rule of law and institutional trust on one side. On the other side, we have the public's right to know when the government acts against its own boundaries (albeit secretly). Edward Snowden's situation could be used to conclude that whistleblowing is only justifiable under certain circumstances: when wrong-doing is widespread, the impact is significant, and all internal avenues have been exhausted. Looking at the situation in this way, Snowden's action may not seem so much treason or heroic. Instead, it appears to be a risky decision where the cost was known and he felt that the value of the truth was worth that cost.

essay_student_10_luna.text: The green light on the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock in F. Scott Fitzgerald's 1925 novel *The Great Gatsby* is representative of Jay Gatsby's dreams, particularly his hopes of being with Daisy again and reliving their past. Gatsby lives in West Egg on the other side of the bay from Daisy's residence in East Egg. Gatsby often stares out and reaches for the small green light on Daisy's dock. The light seems to be within touching distance but there's water between the two of them, which is meant to be representative of the emotional, social and temporal distances between Gatsby and Daisy. Gatsby believes that he can overcome these distances with money and so he builds an elaborate house, throws lavish parties, and makes himself rich to attract Daisy. The green light is representative of the American Dream, too, as Gatsby feels that happiness lies just beyond his grasp. He--as so many other successful people in life--feels that the attainment of one more goal will finally complete him. The green light is a representation of hope, new life, and aspiration but it also can be associated with wealth and so it helps to associate Gatsby's dream of Daisy with his belief that he can buy love and status with money. Nick Carraway ultimately comes to the conclusion that Gatsby's dream is based on an idealized past rather than any reality. He's not just seeking Daisy in 1922. He wants to re-experience the romance he felt for her before he went off to World War I and before she married Tom. Gatsby's infamous remark that the past can be repeated shows how very much he misinterprets hope for possibility. By the novel's end Gatsby is dead, Daisy has deserted him and the green light is still shining over the water on the other side of the bay. It becomes more than a representation of Gatsby's dream alone and becomes representative of the unending chase for a dreamed-of future that the country is engaged in. Fitzgerald's final image of people grasping forward, but also being forced back is representative of both the inspiring quality of the green light and its tragic nature. On the one hand, it represents something to strive for for individuals; on the other, it can make people unable to face reality.

Scott Fitzgerald is a green light which symbolizes Jay Gatsby's aspirations, particularly the aspiration of being with Daisy again and rekindling their former love.
