The invasion of Russia by Napoleon in 1812 wasn't inevitable. It was a disaster born out of choices. Foremost, Napoleon's choices. The Russian invasion of Napoleon was a consequence of political disagreement that did not warrant such war. Russia's Tsar Alexander I left the Continental System, which was Napoleon's blockade of Great Britain, because it was choking Russia's trade of goods like lumber and tallow. Napoleon didn't want to come to terms. Nor did he want compromise. So he marshalled up the Grande Armée with some 600,000 men. The largest army that Europe had ever seen. And on June 24, 1812, he crossed over the Neman river.

The Russian invasion was a disaster that was preventable. First, the timing was foolhardy. He invaded late in June, hoping to win the decisive battle and get Alexander to beg for peace within weeks. But the Russians under Barclay de Tolly and then Mikhail Kutuzov weren't going to let him trap them. They retreated east. Burning their supplies. The campaign turned into a game of cat and mouse. Napoleon arrived at Moscow in September. (After winning the expensive Battle of Borodino on Sept. 7. It resulted in some 70,000 casualties on both sides). But Moscow was in flames and Alexander didn't want to negotiate. A man as clever as Napoleon should have had contingencies for just such an event. But he wasted over a month in Moscow waiting on a letter which he didn't get. Until the winter arrived and a retreat became necessary.

Secondly, the logistics were deliberately insufficient. Napoleon wanted to use a combination of magazines and foraging to feed his army. But the Russian scorched earth policy and the distances were overwhelming that. There were tens of thousands of horses that died. And typhus and dysentery wracked the ranks. Before any major battle took place. It's estimated that of the 600,000 who went into Russia, less than 100,000 came out. If Napoleon had smaller forces with assured supply or even just wanted to have a limited campaign that targeted Lithuania and Belorussia, then he could've had a negotiated settlement without the disaster.

The case can be made that Napoleon as hegemon of Europe had to enforce the Continental System. That if he'd allowed Russia to flaunt it, then it could've caused Austria and Prussia to jump ship too. There's merit to this argument, but it only tells you why the Russian invasion happened. Not how it happened. There were other options. Such as putting the diplomatic squeeze on. Or showing a force of arms in Poland. Or even having a smaller scale punitive campaign.

So, yes, it was a preventable disaster. Born out of overconfidence and poor intelligence. And born out of Napoleon's inability to foresee that an enemy would simply not play his game. It wasn't so much that Russia beat Napoleon. As much as it was his own assumptions which beat him.

Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 was not a foregone conclusion. It was a result of actions and decisions made, and, most importantly, made by Napoleon. The invasion came as a result of a political dispute (unworthy of such a massive conflict, in my opinion) of Russia's Tsar Alexander I's decision to withdraw from Napoleon's Continental System (Napoleon's blockade of Britain) as it was choking off Russian commerce (goods like timber and tallow). Rather than negotiating or even compromising, Napoleon chose to raise his Grande Armée (roughly 600,000 men and the biggest army ever seen in Europe up until that point) and cross the Neman river on June 24th, 1812. 
 It's clear from all the events how avoidable this disaster was. One: he took a huge risk by invading late in the month of June. He was hoping to force the Russian's hand for a decisive battle and compel Alexander into seeking peace within a few weeks. But Barclay de Tolly, and later Mikhail Kutuzov of the Russian Army, didn't want to be tied down and fought a game of retreat and destruction to the east. It became a game of tag instead of a war. It wasn't until September (Napoleon reached Moscow) that he achieved a victory (although costly: he took the battle of Borodino on September 7th. There were roughly 70,000 casualties total). He arrived to a Moscow that was on fire and Alexander's refusal to negotiate. A man of Napoleon's genius should've had contingencies for such events; instead he spent more than a month in Moscow waiting on a letter (which never came) until winter forced a withdrawal. 
 Two: Napoleon knowingly sent his army on a logistically impossible invasion. Napoleon's intention was that his men would be sustained by a mix of magazines and foraging. But Russia's scorched earth policy and long distances made this an impossibility. Tens of thousands of horses perished. Typhus and Dysentary tore through the army before a major battle even occurred. Historians estimate that of the 600,000 men who went into Russia, only around 100,000 returned. If Napoleon had sent a more modest force and ensured the lines of supply or even run a limited invasion to seek a negotiated settlement to Lithuania/Belorussia, he might've avoided disaster. 
 Some people point out how Napoleon as hegemon of Europe was compelled to enforce the Continental System and if Russia was let to flout this, it would've given Austria and Prussia a reason to jump ship. While there's truth in this, it doesn't address how the invasion was carried out. He could've used diplomatic pressure or a show of strength in Poland. Even a more limited punitive campaign could've been run. 
 Ultimately, it was a disaster that could've been avoided. A disaster caused by overconfidence, lack of good intelligence and his failure to consider that someone might just say "I'm not playing your game". Russia didn't really beat him on the battlefield; it beat him in his own mind.

On the evening of 9 November 1989, a slip of the tongue by the spokesman of the GDR, Günter Schabowski, when he claimed that new rules on travel would come into force "immediately" (though the powers that be really meant to open the borders but with a delay and in a controlled way) led masses of people to converge on crossing points such as Bornholmer Strasse. Border soldiers found themselves confused and without instructions: so they allowed people to pass. Within a few hours, thousands of East and West Berliners were dancing on the Wall near the Brandenburg Gate, pounding chunks out of the Wall with hammers.

The end of the Wall was the logical endpoint of a long period of changes and pressures. The policies of glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring) introduced by Mikhail Gorbachev in the Soviet Union weakened the control of Moscow over the Eastern European satellite states. In 1989 he made clear that the Soviet Union wouldn't use force to support the puppet regimes as it did in Hungary in 1956 or in Czechoslovakia in 1968. Since May of that year Hungary had removed the border fence with Austria and allowed GDR people to cross from East to West by that new route. But, besides the Hungarian changes, big demonstrations were occurring also in East Germany. The "Mondays demonstrations" in Leipzig were becoming very large since they reached a participation of over 70,000 people on 9th of October. In the beginning of November, the demonstrations in East Berlin were reaching over half a million people. The stern ruler of East Germany since 1971, Erich Honecker, had to step down in mid-October. His successor Egon Krenz couldn't stop the process.

The consequences were rapid and deep. By 3rd of October 1990, just 12 months later, East Germany and West Germany were formally united into a new state, reunified under the leadership of Chancellor Helmut Kohl. The fall of the Wall also triggered the fast fall of communist regimes in the Eastern Bloc: the Velvet Revolution in Czechoslovakia was rapidly successful in a few weeks. In December 1989 the communist regime in Romania, under Nicolae Ceaușescu, fell dramatically. In the economic field, reunification required big transfers of trillions of DM to modernise the former East Germany, and this is still a matter of economic debate decades later. In the political field, the fall of the Wall is considered a key moment of the end of the Cold War. The Cold War came to an official end with the fall of the Soviet Union in December 1991. A mere slip of the tongue during a press conference turned out to be a key breaking moment in the history of the 20th Century.

East German spokesman Günter Schabowski mistakenly announced on November 9, 1989 that the new rules allowing travel would go into effect "immediately" -- though it was meant to be a later, staged opening. People rushed to cross points such as Bornholmer Strasse, and the border guards, overwhelmed and without orders, allowed people to cross. Hours later, thousands of East and West Berliners danced on top of the Berlin Wall near the Brandenburg Gate, and used hammers to break pieces off.

The collapse of the Berlin Wall didn't happen by accident. It was a long time coming. Policies such as Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika had weakened Moscow's hold on Eastern Europe. In 1989, Gorbachev had made it clear that the Soviet Union was unlikely to interfere militarily, in the usual way, to shore up the satellite regimes (unlike the 1956 Hungarian Revolution or the 1968 Czechoslovakian invasion). That May, the Hungarians had torn down the border fence to Austria, and East Germans now had a new escape route to the west. Huge protests were happening in East Germany. The so-called Monday Demonstrations in Leipzig reached over 70,000 by October 9, while crowds in East Berlin had swelled to over half a million in early November. The hardline leader of East Germany, Erich Honecker -- in power since 1971 -- was forced to step down in mid-October. And his successor Egon Krenz was in over his head as things unraveled.

The effects were quick and profound. Within a year, East and West Germany were officially reunified on October 3, 1990, under the leadership of Chancellor Helmut Kohl. It also triggered the domino effect of the collapse of communist regimes in Eastern Europe. The Czechoslovak "Velvet Revolution" was successful in weeks, while Nicolae Ceaușescu's regime was violently toppled in Romania in December 1989. The reunification of East and West Germany was expensive, with trillions of deutschmarks needed to modernize the East -- a debate that continues among economists decades later. Symbolically, the fall of the Berlin Wall is often seen as the end of the Cold War, which would be formalized when the Soviet Union itself collapsed in December 1991. A slip of the tongue during a press conference had turned into one of the great fault lines of 20th century history.

Uber driving in 2020 seemed like freedom. And then came the COVID-19 pandemic. The freedom to be an Uber driver became freedom to be exploited. You can set your own hours as an Uber driver. You can decline rides. You can just use the app and make money with no boss to speak of. This was very attractive to many, especially to those who lost jobs in restaurants or retail, or in offices. But as an Uber driver, you also have to pay for gas and car maintenance and insurance. You have to pay for the lost time when you're waiting for someone to arrive. You are a contractor, and so you don't have paid sick leave and unemployment and health insurance from your employer.

Things were especially dire in March and April of 2020 as the lockdown restrictions really limited travel. In April, Uber says its ride business was down about 80 percent from the previous year. And drivers were still vulnerable to being a vector for the coronavirus from one passenger to the next. Uber pledged $24 million in assistance for Uber drivers and delivery workers across the globe. But the support was scarce and not always accessible to many workers. There were other requirements around masks and safety protocols. Some of the burden of protection fell onto the drivers.

In 2020, this conversation was especially prominent in California. Assembly Bill 5, enacted in 2019, made it harder for companies to label workers as contractors. Uber and Lyft emphasized that drivers want to be independent. And they waged a big battle for Proposition 22. And on November 3, 2020, Californians voted for it. Drivers using apps like Uber and Lyft could be independent contractors but would receive some benefits such as a subsidy for healthcare and payment by the amount of time you're driving (engaged). And proponents, such as Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, framed the law as a way to maintain flexibility. Critics as saying this was a way for the profitable technology companies to avoid employment costs.

So Uber driving in 2020 was a mixture of freedom and exploitation. Freedom to control your schedule but not to control fares or expenses or health or benefits. The ultimate flexibility would have to come from drivers maintaining that right to schedule while also having more protection from sickness and accidents and income volatility. The lesson of 2020 is that freedom is not all that great if you have to bear nearly all the risks and companies have most of the power.

For Uber drivers in 2020, freedom and exploitation coexist. The Uber app gives you control over your schedule. But it doesn't give you control over your fares, or costs, or risks to your health, or your benefits. To get the kind of freedom we want, drivers need to continue to set their own hours, while also having far better protection from getting sick or hurt, or from economic insecurity. 2020 has shown us that independence is not so meaningful when you're forced to absorb almost all of the risk, while the corporations control most of the power.

Toni Morrison shows in Beloved (1987) that the pain of slavery does not end with the emancipation. The horror of slavery lives on in memory and becomes a ghost of its own that haunts the present, much like the ghost haunting 124 Bluestone Road. Escaped slave Sethe has settled in Cincinnati in 1873, 18 years after her escape from Sweet Home plantation in Kentucky. There is no way to avoid what keeps coming back to her in what she calls "rememory". The word is an invention of Morrison's. This lets us know that memory is not something personal, but a possessing force which exists somewhere in the world, waiting to spring a surprise on anyone who walks by. Sethe makes Denver aware of the fact that, even though she might forget her shame of Sweet Home, "it's still out there". Still, it is a place where the past can still happen to you.

Morrison carefully does not disclose the true horror that forms the center of the novel: the murder of Sethe's 2 year old daughter in 1855 to avoid her returning to slavery. Furthermore she makes the point that literature can be an act of remembrance. The ending of the book is "This is not a story to pass on". This paradox is both a warning of not to repeat the story. In her novel Beloved (1987), Toni Morrison shows how the horrors of slavery go beyond the time of emancipation. The trauma continues in the form of memory. It's the ghost in 124 Bluestone Road. In 1873 Cincinnati, eighteen years after she ran away from the Sweet Home plantation in Kentucky, the escaped slave Sethe can't avoid the 'rememory' (her word) that keeps coming back. Morrison's term for this reflects her view that memories aren't merely things we own: they are forces we contain within ourselves and that live in the world as well, ready to spring a trap on anyone who comes along. 'Even if you forget the disgrace of Sweet Home,' Sethe cautions her daughter Denver, 'it's still out there.' Sweet Home is the place where the past can still happen to you.

In Beloved, Morrison purposely doesn't show the reader Sethe's most horrific act: killing her two-year-old daughter in 1855 to save her from being taken back into slavery. Instead, the story is revealed in bits and pieces the way real traumatic memories occur. Sethe can't tell her story chronologically; it keeps coming back in fragments, connected to certain sensory cues. Once Beloved appears in 124 in the flesh (the dead daughter? come back to age she would've been? about 19?), Morrison makes the concept of the past not staying dead literal. Beloved feeds off Sethe's stories. She wants to hear them over and over. The experience of telling and remembering becomes almost too much.

But Morrison stresses that memory, no matter how awful it is, is essential. The reason the ghost can thrive is because the community has deserted Sethe: the ghost takes over Baby Suggs's abandoned sermons in the Clearing. Only when thirty women come to sing and pray at 124 can Beloved be exorcised. In dedicating the book to 'Sixty Million and more', it's clear Sethe's story represents the collective story that's been repressed. By putting a story to things that couldn't be told, Morrison claims that in order to go forward, people must face what happened to them. Literature can be a means of remembering. The acetone (nail polish remover) smell is completely fine for a young starter. It's actually the smell of fermentation which means you're doing something right! 
 
 The gist: Once you get to day 48-72, the wild yeasts and bacteria in your flour start producing acetic acid and esters as they eat the starches. Then, when your starter's food runs out in between feedings, you see a change in the bacteria activity leading to acetone-like compounds being produced. Especially true for whole grain (rye/whole wheat) flours, which ferment more and more aggressively than AP flours 
 
 Solution: 
 
 1. More frequent feedings. Feed every 12hrs for the next 3-4 days (rather than 24hr feedings). 1:1:1 ratio by weight (eg. 50g starter, 50g flour, 50g water (around 78F) 
 
 2. Check if your starter is too thin. When it's too thin, acids build up quicker. Slow down things a bit by making it slightly thicker (equal weight) 
 
 3. If your counter is hotter than 75F (eg. oven, hot kitchen), this can speed things up too so the starter is eating too much too quickly. Try to keep it 68-75F. Mine's next to the coffee machine away from stove and it was a game-changer. 
 
 What to expect. Sometimes, the smell can actually get *worse* around days 4-6. Could start smelling like gym socks, puke etc. as the different bacteria fight. Don't freak out. Don't throw it out. By days 7-10, most starters will get to a nice yeast smell. Slight tangy, apple cider vinegar smell. Consistent good rise (eg. doubling every 4-6hrs after a feeding) 
 
 When should you worry? Only when you see pink/orange streaks (mold) or fuzzy stuff on the top. Otherwise, don't worry about the acetone smell. Your starter is just hungry! Feed consistently and it'll correct itself. 
 
 Source: Same starter since March 2021. Whenever I let it go too many days without feeding, it'd smell like the nail salon.

datetime.utcnow() (and utcfromtimestamp()) create a naive datetime. It provides UTC wall clock times but removes the tzinfo. There's no way to tell it's a UTC time object. That's why it's deprecated in 3.12! It's all too easy to treat that naive datetime object as local time and make subtle mistakes when comparing it with an aware datetime or calling astimezone() and getting the wrong answer silently.

Instead you need to avoid using utcnow() and instead create an aware datetime:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

Now "now" is an aware datetime with tzinfo=timezone.utc so now.isoformat() will produce "2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983+00:00" rather than the ambiguous "2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983"

If you're on Python 3.11+ "datetime.UTC" is a shortcut for timezone.utc

Other suggestions for 2024+:

Never mix naive and aware datetimes when comparing (Python will complain with TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes but it's nice that it raises an exception but now you have to be consistent)

If you ever need something other than UTC (e.g. you want America/Chicago or Asia/Tokyo) then use zoneinfo from the standard library (3.9+) rather than importing pytz.
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
chicago = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("America/Chicago"))

Store timestamps in your database as UTC (can be aware or explicit UTC naive - just be consistent) and only convert to a local timezone at the display layer

If using Django, USE_TZ=True with django.utils.timezone.now() will give you the right thing. It follows this same pattern.

So datetime.now(timezone.utc) is the non-deprecated direct replacement for datetime.utcnow()

datetime.utcnow(), as well as utcfromtimestamp() are meant to provide a naive datetime object. That is, it'll give you the utc time of the current wall-clock, but then remove tzinfo. No way to indicate that it's in UTC. This is why it's deprecated (3.12). Because it's really easy to then think "ooh, a naive datetime! This must be a local datetime". And then you're silently getting the wrong result if you compare it to an aware datetime, or astimezone().

You should just not use utcnow(), and just create an aware datetime:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

now will have tzinfo=timezone.utc. So now.isoformat() will output 2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983+00:00 (not just 2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983, which could be anything). (In 3.11+ datetime.UTC is shorthand for timezone.utc)

A few other things in 2024+ you may wanna do:
- Avoid mixing naive and aware datetimes in comparisons. Python will raise "TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes". So that's nice that it doesn't just go silently wrong. But you really have to be consistent.
- If you want something beyond just UTC. Like you need America/Chicago or Asia/Tokyo. Then use the stdlib zoneinfo (3.9+), instead of importing pytz.

from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

chicago = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("America/Chicago"))

- Store your timestamps as utc in the db. (aware, or explicit utc-naive. Just be consistent) - Only do zone conversion to a local zone at the display time.

- If you're using django, then "USE_TZ = True" + "django.utils.timezone.now()" already does the right thing and follows this same pattern.

So yeah, datetime.now(timezone.utc) is the direct replacement for datetime.utcnow(). And it's not deprecated.

As a freelancer, I would advise that you set aside 6-12 months worth of critical personal expenses (not a random dollar amount). Given the income volatility, I think the upper end is more realistic than the traditional 3 months.

So if you are living in Portland OR and your super bare bones monthly expenses are...

Rent/utils: $1800 
 Health insurance/medical: $500 
 Food: $500 
 Transportation: $250 
 Minimum debts/other critical stuff: $150

...then your critical monthly expenses are $3200/month. And so you should be looking to have $19200 for a 6-month emergency fund. $28800 gives you a better buffer for 9 months.

You should probably have 3 different accounts. 1 for emergency (job gap, sick, major surprise expenses), 1 for tax (pay the quarterly taxes to federal/state for estimated taxes) and 1 for business (software, hardware replacement, subcontractors, client slow payment, etc.). 
 Otherwise you might end up with a big surprise tax bill or dead laptop and your "emergency fund" could look larger than it actually is.

Determine the amount for the goal by starting from your least feasible minimum monthly expenses (not average lifestyle). Try to make your own paycheck something consistent. Like $4k a month out of the business account. Put crazy good months into savings. Then rebuild the fund if you use it. Store it in an accessible FDIC savings account (not invested).

Note that the CFPB explicitly mentions emergency funds as beneficial for irregular income folks. The FDIC mentions 3-6 months as a general rule. They do mention that if you are especially volatile in employment you should go as far as 6 months+ [CFPB guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/an-essential-guide-to-building-an-emergency-fund/) [FDIC guidance](https://www.fdic.gov/consumer-resource-center/2025-01/saving-unexpected-and-your-future)

Could be a number of things.  But the fact that its happening specifically on a 2009 civic makes it more likely it's one of a few things. 
 Most likely culprit is worn brake pads.  It's not unusual for Civics (06-11) to wear front pads out around 40-60k miles.  You'll hear grinding if your pads are all the way down to metal backing plate.  Often its worse downhill.  You're using more brake force for longer times.  More heat, more pressure.  If it's grinding under braking.  Start there.  Take a wheel off.  Or see through the wheels spokes.  The brake pad friction material should be at least 3mm thick.  If your rotor face looks scored, grooved, your pads have been metal on metal for a while.  You'll need rotors as well.  Expect $150-250 per axle at an indy shop for pads and rotors. 
 Why specifically downhill? 
 Two reasons. 
 1) Heat.  Constant downhill braking (especially on a long downhill grade) can build up heat in your rotors.  If they're warped.  Or have uneven deposits.  You'll have pulsating.  Sometimes a groaning or grinding noise.  Warped rotors are common.  If your brake pads weren't cared for at some point in the cars life. 
 2) Weight transfer.  When braking downhill more weight is transferred to the front brakes.  Makes any existing pad/rotor wear noises more pronounced. 
 Other possible causes: 
 Glazed pads.  If the previous owner rode their brakes a lot.  It could cause the pad surface to harden.  Grinding/growling under load. 
 Sticking caliper.  Seized caliper slide pin is not uncommon on 8th gen Civics.  It'll drag your brake pad against your rotor and it'll grind.  Especially if its hot.  Look for one wheel that's dustier/hotter than the others after a drive. 
 Rust on your rotors.  If your car sits for days.  It can build up rust on the surface.  You'll hear it.  Usually its gone away after a few stops.  But if it's a constant grinding.  Not the cause. 
 Dont let it go.  If it's grinding.  Its making metal to metal contact.  Each week you let it go will eat up your rotors.  And could lead to caliper damage.  If your handy.  Changing pads and rotors on a civic is very doable yourself.  2 hours with basic tools.  If not, get it into a shop this week. 
 Quick test.  Does it grind specifically when applying the brakes?  Or does it also grind when you're coasting downhill with your foot off the brake pedal?  If it grinds when coasting downhill.  Probably a wheel bearing or dragging caliper.  Not the brake pads.  Makes a big difference to your mechanic.

Not usually. This catches a lot of people off guard because of changes in 2018. 
 If you are a W2 employee (based on your idea of "working remotely for my employer") then TCJA suspended the itemized miscellaneous deduction for unreimbursed employee business expenses (including the home office deduction) for 2018 - 2025. Whether you are in for 1 day a week or 5 days...as a W2 employee you just can't deduct it on the federal return. Period. Even if your employer mandates the hybrid situation. Even if they don't provide you with a permanent desk when you are in the office. 
 Ways that could affect things: 
 1. If you are 1099 contractor or have self-employment income on the side. If you have any self-employment income (for example you have a side hustle of freelance consulting you do from that home office) then you can deduct the business use of your home for the self employment income using Form 8829. Again, the home has to be used in a "regular and exclusive" use. (i.e. if you use the home office as a guest room on the weekends it doesn't count). 
 2. State taxes - There are some states (CA, NY, PA, AL, AR) that still permit unreimbursed employee expense deduction on the state return even though it's been suspended at the federal level. You'll want to look into your specific state rules for 2025. 
 3. Employer not reimbursing you? Do they have an "accountable plan"? If they do reimburse you (for internet, a monitor, etc) for some of the expenses as part of an accountable plan. Then it's not treated as income to you for tax purposes. So it's better (for all intents and purposes) than if you deducted it anyway. 
 For your typical hybrid situation W2 employee. You can't deduct home office on the federal return. Look up your state. See if your employer would directly reimburse you for the expenses. 
 *not* specific tax advice for you - you can get a CPA to check on your specific situation based on the whole return.

2-inch: A metal self-adhesive drywall patch instead of just trying to fill the hole with joint compound.

First, remove any loose paper. Use a utility knife to clean up and square any rough edges. Clean off dust. Place a 4-inch (or larger) metal mesh patch centered over the hole. Press firmly to get a good flat surface. If the damage is near a corner or a stud, watch out that the patch is not crossing an uneven surface.

Apply setting type joint compound such as 45 minute Easy Sand. Use a 6-inch taping knife and feather out the compound at least 3 inches past the patch. Allow to harden and scrape down any ridges. Add another (thinner) coat. You may have to add a final skim coat to fully cover the patch.

Once the final coat is dry (usually overnight) give a light sanding using 150 or 220 grit sand paper. Run your hand over the surface and if you feel an edge. Add more compound. Don't try to sand it hard. Clean off the dust. Prime the area with drywall primer. Paint it using the same color wall paint.

Since the hole was caused by a door knob you need to install a doorstop or hinge pin stop once you've done the repair. A door knob striking the wall generally means that a wall-mounted rubber stop is the best choice. If the hole is near an electrical outlet or switch be sure to turn off the circuit before cutting or sanding. Stay away from using screws in that area.

For a 2-inch hole, don't try to mud it closed. Instead, get a metal drywall patch with a self-adhesive backing.

First, cut out the loose paper. Neaten up rough edges with your utility knife. Remove dust. Center a metal mesh patch (4-inch or larger) over the hole. Press it firmly to flatten it. If your hole is in a corner or beside a stud, be sure that the patch isn't spanning an uneven surface.

Put setting type joint compound (45-minute Easy Sand, for example) over the patch. Use a 6-inch taping knife. Blend at least 3-inches outside the patch. Allow it to set. Scrape high spots. Put on a second coat. It should be thinner. You may want to put on a third skim coat to completely conceal the patch.

Once the last coat has dried (usually over night), sand gently with 150-220 grit sandpaper. Finger over the spot to check. If there's a ridge, put more compound on it, not a heavy sanding. Dust off. Apply drywall primer to the repair spot. Paint with the same color as the wall.

Since this is a door knob hole, add a doorstop or hinge pin stop after you make the repair. If the knob is banging the wall, a wall mounted rubber stop is probably your best bet. If the hole is near an electric outlet or switch, shut down the circuit before cutting or sanding. Don't drive screws near there either.

Well, great news. At age 55, 120/80 is really really healthy. That's pretty much the "ideal" value. 
 American heart association says <120/80 is "normal" and 120-129 sytolic and <80 diastolic "elevated" Stage 1 is 130/80 and stage 2 140/90. You're right at the high end of the "normal" range. That's where a lot of 55 year olds would be. Blood pressure will generally rise as arteries become stiffer with age. So it's really great that at age 55 you're still around 120/80. It's not something to be concerned about. 
 A few things to note though: 
 1. It's only a single reading. Blood pressure can fluctuate a lot during the day. Also it can change with stress, caffeine, sleep, talking during the measurement etc. So if you got that 120/80 from a single measurement at a pharmacy or at the doctor and it's a stressful situation. Try taking a few more measurements over a week or so. Sit down, have your arm supported, take a 5 minute break and then see what your average blood pressure is like. 
 2. In addition to blood pressure number, ask your doctor about your 10 year risk factors. You're 55 now. So they should also consider your cholesterol, blood glucose, family history, smoking, weight etc. You can have good blood pressure but bad risk factors.

The surefire solution is baking soda paste, takes about 10 minutes:
 - 3 baking soda to 1 water to form paste (say 3 tbps to 1 tbps for a 18" standard board)
 - Apply paste to the board with a clean rag or the cut side of a half lemon, in the grain. Let sit 5-10 minutes
 - Rinse with hot water, immediately dry (edge up so it doesn't warp)
 
For long-lasting smells, you can use course salt as a physical "scrub". Sprinkle salt on the board. Then scrub with half lemon to use the salt as the abrasive. The lemon (citric acid) helps remove sulfur compounds to get rid of the 'stickyness' of the smell of garlic (it's the allicin/degradation byproducts that cause the 'garlic breath'). Salt helps pull anything out of the wood's grain. Rinse and dry.
 
For boards that have accumulated the smell of garlic/onion for many months, you may want to use the baking soda and water to soak for a longer time (1 tbps baking soda in quart of warm water). Soak (or cover in baking soda paste) for 15-20 minutes. Then scrub with a stiff brush against the grain.
 
- don't throw a wood board in the dishwasher or soak it for hours. It'll crack or delaminate, especially end grain
- avoid using plain vinegar as a first option since it can take away the natural wood oils from constant use. It's OK to use it occasionally, diluted 1:1 with water. Wipe/rinse and do immediately.
 - once dry, apply a food-grade mineral oil or a board creme (blend of beeswax and mineral oil) so that you re-condition the wood and make it 'less smelly' next time (the better it's oiled, the less porous it'll be).
 
If you often use garlic, have a small board for strongly smelling foods so you don't get this problem with your main board.

The best remedy is baking soda paste, works in 10 mins or so.

1) 3:1 ratio baking soda: water (make paste of 3:1, say 3 tbsp baking soda: 1 tbsp water for typical 18" cutting board)

2) Scrub into cutting board with clean cloth or cut side of half a lemon (with grain)

Let soak in for 5-10 mins

3) Wash off with hot water. Dry immediately (place on end to avoid warping)

If you still get a smell, then you can try coarse salt as a mechanical cleaner. Sprinkle a layer of course salt on board, then scrub with half lemon, using salt as the abrasive.

The citric acid in the lemon will help neutralize garlic sulfur compounds (the ones that make garlic "stick"--same break down products as garlic breath (allicin)).

Salt will help remove residues from within the wood grain. Wash off and dry.

A deeper clean can help a cutting board that has soaked in garlic/onion odor over many months. Mix 1 tbsp baking soda into 1 quart warm water. Soak (or cover in baking soda paste) for 15-20 minutes. Then scrub with stiff brush, against the grain.

Things to avoid:

-Don't put a wood board in the dishwasher, or soak for extended periods. Especially for end-grain cutting boards, board will crack or delaminate.

-Avoid straight vinegar as first option. May dull natural wood oils with repeated use. Occasionally, can be ok to use diluted 1:1 with water. Wipe off and rinse quickly afterwards.

-After drying, you can apply some food-safe mineral oil or a board cream (beeswax/mineral oil mixture). That will recondition the wood. Actually, the board will be less prone to odors next time as well, since a well oiled wood surface has less porosity.

If you use a lot of garlic, maybe you can just have a small cutting board for pungent ingredients, and never have this problem with your main cutting board.

If you have a `users` table with an `email` column, first you group by email and you filter groups that have multiple rows in them:

```sql
SELECT
    email,
    COUNT(*) as duplicate_count
FROM users
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC, email;
```

That will give you all the duplicated emails and how many times they appear (e.g. if email `alex@example.com` appears 3 times you get something like:

```text
alex@example.com | 3
```

If you want to consider emails as duplicates also ignoring capitalization and spaces around them, you can normalize in your query:

```sql
SELECT
    LOWER(TRIM(email)) as normalized_email,
    COUNT(*) as duplicate_count
FROM users
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC;
```

Now if you want to get all the user records that are being duplicated you can use a derived table:

```sql
SELECT u.*
FROM users u
JOIN (
    SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) as normalized_email
    FROM users
    WHERE email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
) as d
    ON d.normalized_email = LOWER(TRIM(u.email))
ORDER BY d.normalized_email, u.id;
```

This is still a normal aggregation query (for 2M rows) but you can help yourself with an index. If your database supports it, you can create an index over the normalized value. If you're using PostgreSQL you can do:

```sql
CREATE INDEX users_email_normalized_idx
ON users (LOWER(TRIM(email)));
```

For future inserts, if you want to disallow duplication, you enforce the uniqueness. If you're using PostgreSQL:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_unique_idx
ON users (LOWER(TRIM(email)))
WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
```

So before you apply that constraint you should clean up or decide what to do with the existing duplicates, otherwise index creation will fail if you have any duplicate normalized email addresses.

Suppose you have a table 'users' with a column 'email'. Group by email and take groups of more than 1 rows:

select email, count(*) as duplicate_count
from users
where email is not null
group by email
having count(*) > 1
order by duplicate_count desc, email;

So this query will show you all email addresses with duplicate occurrences and how many times it duplicated. If you have alex@example.com which appears 3 times you'll see:

alex@example.com | 3

In case you want to treat email address as duplicates regardless of case, extra spaces then normalize it inside of query:

select lower(trim(email)) as normalized_email, count(*) as duplicate_count
from users
where email is not null
group by lower(trim(email))
having count(*) > 1
order by duplicate_count desc;

To see specific user records that participate in those duplicates use derived table:

select u.* 
from users u
join 
 (
  select lower(trim(email)) as normalized_email
  from users
  where email is not null
  group by lower(trim(email))
  having count(*) > 1
 ) d
 on lower(trim(u.email)) = d.normalized_email
 order by d.normalized_email, u.id;

2M is still standard aggregation query but you can help it by index. Create index on normalized value if your database allows it (for e.g. PostgreSQL)

create index users_email_normalized_idx on users (lower(trim(email)));

and for future inserts make it unique if you don't allow duplicates (in postgresql, for e.g.)

create unique index users_email_unique_idx on users (lower(trim(email))) where email is not null;

Note that you want to clean up or make decision on duplicate rows before you apply this constraint as it will fail in the moment of index creation, because of duplicate normalized addresses.

MEMORANDUM
 To: Maria Delgado, Chief Financial Officer
 From: James Okonkwo, Chief Information Security Officer
 Date: March 14, 2025
 Re: FY 2026 Cybersecurity Budget Request - Increase from $4.2M to $4.7M

Purpose
 The objective of this memo is to request a 12% increase in the budget for the Cybersecurity department for FY2026. I am asking that we increase the budget from $4.2M to $4.7M. This memo provides an overview of justification, allocation and anticipated outcomes.

Justification
There are three items that require an increase in budget:
1. Regulatory. Increased monitoring and documentation is required for audit readiness (SOC 2 Type II) and the new state privacy law which will take effect Jan 1, 2026. Incremental compliance costs - $180K
2. Threat. There was an increase in targeted phishing campaigns (14 in FY2025, compared to 6 the previous year) and 2 close-calls with ransomware in Q3 2025. We need to renew our SIEM licensing and the 24x7 monitoring contract with SentinelWatch. This contract ends in August 2025, and needs to be renewed at a 9% premium.
3. Business Growth. The Denver office opens in October 2025. We now have 850 heads. There has been an increase of approximately 20% in our attack surface since the FY2024 budget was established.

How I intend to allocate additional $500K
 a. Renewal of SIEM & increased monitoring coverage. - $220K
 b. One additional Security Engineer (1 FTE, fully loaded) - $165K
 c. MFA upgrade & endpoint detection tools. - $75K
 d. Employee security awareness training - all offices. - $40K

Alternatives Considered
 It is not an option to postpone SIEM renewal. This would leave us with a coverage gap which would not be covered by our cyber-insurance. This would leave us with a potential liability of $2M which is not covered. We considered outsourcing the additional engineering position. The cost of managed services quotes were 30% higher over a 3 year period than an in-house option.

Anticipated Outcomes
 This investment should result in 100% compliance with audits in Q2 FY2026. MTTD (Mean Time to Detection of threats) should decrease from 6 hours to less than 90 mins. The zero-trust rollout will be complete by June 2026.

Please let me know if you would like a walk-through of the details. I am also happy to present to the Finance Committee at the April 22 meeting if needed.

MEMORANDUM

To: All Employees From: Dana Whitfield - VP HR Date: November 14, 2024 Subject: Update to Parental Leave Policy (effective January 1, 2025)

I'm happy to share that our paid parental leave benefit will be increased to 16 weeks effective January 1, 2025 after a competitive benefits benchmarking analysis we completed this fall.

We did a benchmark study in Q3 comparing parental leave policies at 12 peer companies within our industry (including our 3 closest competitors for talent). Median paid parental leave was 14 weeks and we saw some companies recently increasing to 16+ weeks. Our old 8-week policy puts us in the bottom quartile, and it was a reason for 23% of offer-decline acceptances in our recruiting exit surveys over the last 18 months.

What's changing

Effective January 1, 2025, all eligible full-time employees that become parents via birth, adoption or foster placement will be eligible for an increase from 8 to 16 weeks of paid parental leave. This includes the following details:

- Can be taken within 12 months of child arrival
- Open to all parents (regardless of gender / care giving role)
- Can be continuous leave or split into 2 separate chunks with manager approval
- Employees that have already started their leave on or after 10/1/2024 can choose to continue under the new policy if they contact HR.

Job protection still applies with FMLA and relevant state laws (we're now above and beyond the legal requirements)

What's staying the same

Our short-term disability (which is for birth mothers, up to 8 weeks long and is provided through Lincoln financial) is still separate and runs in parallel to the initial weeks of parental leave. The existing 4 weeks of paid leave for family medical emergencies to provide care giving remains unchanged.

Budget impact

The expanded parental leave policy is estimated to have a $740K/year impact. This was approved on 11/6 from the Finance Committee as part of FY2025 benefits budget. This is expected to be somewhat offset by decreased turnover (we see an avg replacement cost of 42% of salary for departing employees in our 2023 analysis)

If you have questions, reach out to hr@company.com or ask at all-hands meeting on 12/3. We'll update the policy doc on HR portal by 12/15.

Summary We recommend closing the Centerville retail store at the end of the current lease on August 31, 2025. The store has failed to become profitable despite ongoing management focus, expense management and sales improvement efforts. The operating losses are detracting from other higher performing stores and impede us from investing in e-commerce, retention and profitable markets.

In the last 12 months Centerville has produced about $1.2M in sales with about $1.45M in operating costs which gives an annual loss of $250k (estimated). Centerville averages about an 8% YOY drop in monthly sales with increases in rent, personnel, utilities, and inventory carrying cost. In addition the store sees substantially lower traffic than what's needed to support the store's size.

By closing the store at the end of the lease we will eliminate renewal requirements, lowered fixed operating costs and save us from spending about $150k on planned facility/merchandising spending. The net improvement to annual operating income will be about $230k after accounting for one-time costs such as severance, inventory write-downs, relocation, lease exit activities.

We will need to provide at minimum 60 days notice to all Centerville store employees. We will look to provide qualified team members with opportunities to transfer to Riverside and Northgate (where we have open positions). We will shift inventory to other nearby stores and online channel (beginning in June 2025) and conduct a controlled clearance effort (July/Aug). Communicate to customers about continued service via our online store and nearby stores.

Management should officially notify the landlord by 5/31/2025 at the latest. Employee consultations should be done by 6/15. We will close the store at the end of the day on 8/31/2025. This is fiscally responsible, operationally feasible and in alignment with company strategy of focusing on profitable channels and stores.

We suggest closing the Centerville retail store upon the expiration of our lease agreement on August 31st, 2025. Despite consistent efforts from management, cost management, and sales enhancement measures, the Centerville store has consistently been unprofitable. The Centerville store's operating losses are not only preventing higher performing store performance but also preventing our company from investing in our e-commerce, customer retention and profitable markets.

Over the last year, Centerville's sales have been approximately $1.2m, and we've seen their operating expenses to be around $1.45m for a loss of approximately $250k per year. On a monthly basis, the average sales have been dropping around 8% YoY while rent, employee costs, utilities and inventory costs continue to rise. Furthermore, the store traffic is well below what would be needed to sustain the current store footprint.

Opting to close the store upon lease expiration allows us to avoid renewing any obligations on the lease. In addition to avoiding the fixed operating expenses, we would not incur any of the roughly $150k in planned facility and merchandising expenses. With this closure, we expect to see an improvement of approximately $230k to our annual operating income (with consideration to one-time costs such as severance, inventory markdown, relocation and lease exit).

We should provide a minimum of 60 days notice to the employees of the Centerville store. Qualified employees should be considered for relocation to the Riverside and Northgate stores where we have available openings. Inventory should be shifted to our nearby stores and company online starting in June of 2025 with controlled clearance in July and August. We should be communicating the continued service through our online store and to our nearby stores to customers.

Formal notice of this should be delivered to the landlord no later than May 31st, 2025. Employee consultation should be completed by June 15th and we would close the store following the business day on August 31st, 2025. From a financial standpoint, this is the prudent course of action. Operationally it can be managed, and strategically it aligns with our focus on profitable channels and locations.

MEMO

To: All Department Heads & Regional Managers
From: Priya Nair, Director of Human Resources
Date: April 14, 2025
Re: Updated Remote Work Eligibility Changes - Summary of March Staff Survey Results

Purpose
This memo outlines the key results from the March 2025 remote work survey (n=1,240, 82% participation rate) and the updated eligibility changes that will take effect on June 2, 2025.

Survey Highlights
- 74% of respondents prefer a hybrid approach; only 11% express a need to be in the office full-time.
- 87% of responses show either the same or improved self-rated productivity on remote work days.
- The lowest satisfaction levels come from departments with strict in-office requirements (Facilities, Front Desk Services, Print Production)
- 63% of staff identified significant commuting costs ($340/month on average) as an issue.

Updated Policy Effective June 2, 2025

1. Base Hybrid Arrangement: Eligible employees will have access to work up to 3 days (up from 2) remotely per week with manager approval.

2. 100% Remote Classification: Location-independent roles (112 positions in IT, Finance, Marketing currently) can be 100% remote with quarterly performance review.

3. In-Person Roles: Essential in-person roles (building security, mail room, lab technicians at Portland/Denver sites) must stay in office. $75/month commuting stipend.

4. Eligibility: Requires 6 months of tenure (down from 12 months) with a performance rating of at least "Meets Expectations".

Implementation
- Updated hybrid team agreements due to HR by May 16, 2025 for manager review.
- All employees must update their Remote Work Agreement in Workday by May 30, 2025 to the new terms.
- Remote employees within 50 miles of Denver, Austin, Boston offices will need to be onsite for team collaboration days once a month.

Other Points
- Remote arrangements must still follow state tax/labor laws where the employee is working.
- Any requests to move out of state require 60 days notice and will go through HR Legal.
- Please ask questions at hr-policy@company.com or at our all-hands briefing on April 24.
