The company should approve on or before September 21, 2026, its potential purchase of the geothermal assets of TerraFusion Energy for $340mm. The deal hinges upon satisfactory due diligence on the environment, titles, and production. The assets consist of the 48 MW Silver Basin plant near Winnemucca, NV, the 32 MW expansion of Coso Ridge in Inyo Co. CA, and the associated exploration leases for roughly 41,000 acres of land in NV and eastern CA.

The acquisition offer represents an effective $4.25mm per MW of installed capacity for the current and late-stage 80 MW of power. This price is comparable for firm and renewable power supply, especially in the context of the potential access to federal clean energy tax incentives. Plus, the projects could offer 24/7 power capacity. At average contract power rates of $72/MW-hr, initial calculations show that the portfolio could be a revenue opportunity of approximately $58mm in revenue annually (before operating expenses and royalties).

There are several major risks associated with the project: resource exhaustion, permitting delays, water use constraints, and the existing liabilities of TerraFusion with county government and tribal partners. Thus, the deal structure needs to include $290mm at closing and potential earn-out payments of up to $50mm based upon production milestones, permitting successes, and a successful commissioning of the Coso Ridge expansion by 12/31/28.

Prior to execution, the company should insist upon third-party verification of resource potential. The company should review all 37 Federal and state permits. It should also confirm land and mineral titles. The company should also have a maintenance/capital plan over the next five years. The company must obtain PPAs for at least 70% of projected output. The company should reserve a minimum of $35mm for well remediation and for unexpected drilling.

Assuming these conditions are met, the acquisition would enhance the company's renewable power production platform in the western U.S. It would also enhance the firm's capacity for dependable baseload power. It helps the company meet its 2030 goal of reducing carbon emissions. However, unless the acquisition includes a price structure based upon milestones and verified resource potential, we do not recommend the company accept the headline $340mm price for the portfolio.

On September 21, 2026, approve acquisition of geothermal assets from TerraFusion Energy for an estimated $340MM (subject to environmental/title/production due diligence). This portfolio consists of 48 MW Silver Basin (near Winnemucca, NV), 32 MW Coso Ridge expansion (Inyo County, CA), and related exploration leases totaling ~41,000 acres in Nevada and east California.

Implied valuation on the portfolio is an estimated $4.25MM per MW-installed for the 80 MW of operational/late-stage development. This price is competitive for firm/renewable generation and especially attractive as these assets could potentially qualify for federal clean energy tax incentives and offer 24 hour capacity. Rough estimates suggest this portfolio has the potential to deliver ~ $58MM/year of revenue based on an average power price of $72/MWh (not including O&M/royalties).

Key risks include resource decline, permitting, water use restrictions and TerraFusion outstanding county/tribal commitments. Accordingly, transaction structure should include $290MM payable at closing with up to $50MM in earn-out consideration linked to production milestones, permitting status, and successful Coso Ridge expansion commissioning by December 31, 2028.

Acquiror should demand independent reservoir evaluation, review all 37 feds/state permits, confirm land/mineral rights, and a 5 year maintenance/capital plan prior to signing. Management should obtain power purchase agreements to cover at least 70% of projected output and maintain a reserve of at least $35MM for well remediation/unplanned drilling.

Protected, this acquisition would improve western U.S. renewable generation platform, provide firm/base-load generation and support 2030 carbon reduction initiatives. However, without milestone pricing and confirmed resource assessment, do not accept $340MM stated valuation.

paper_section_01_luna.text:
After the 2020 CASP14 evaluation, AlphaFold2 was released and appeared in Nature in 2021. AlphaFold2 was a major breakthrough of protein structure prediction. Evoformer in AlphaFold2 introduced multiple attention and outer product operations to iteratively pass messages between the multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and residue pair level representations. Structure module using invariant point attention (IPA) helped to transform those representations into 3D coordinates. Thanks to the combination of evolution analysis with geometric reasoning and reusing predictions as intermediate results, AlphaFold2 scored a median 92.4 GDT-TS in CASP14. Even for the challenging free modeling tasks, AlphaFold2 achieved a median of 87.0 GDT-TS. IPA was crucial, because the attention mechanism of IPA can focus on the learned 3D points and is invariant to the global rotation and translation. [Jumper et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2)

After AlphaFold2, several variants of attention-based models were proposed. For example, RoseTTAFold of the University of Washington was presented in Science in 2021. RoseTTAFold adopted a three-channel model to simultaneously learn 1D sequence/MSA features, 2D residue pair features, and 3D coordinates. Attention, graph transformer operations, and SE(3)-equivariant layers are used to share the information among different representations. For proteins smaller than 400 residues, the end-to-end model can produce backbone coordinates within about 10 min with RTX 2080 GPU. [Baek et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj8754)

Meanwhile, the protein language models view protein structure prediction as a byproduct of learning sequence-level representation. ESM-2 and ESMFold of Meta use Transformer language model embeddings to structure prediction from single sequence data, which saves the expensive computation of MSAs. ESMFold appeared in Science in 2023 and was applied to ESM Metagenomic Atlas with over 617 M proteins predictions. However, the prediction accuracy generally lags behind AlphaFold2. [Lin et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ade2574)

Most recently, AlphaFold3 appeared in Nature in 2024, which goes beyond protein folding and provides biomolecular interaction modeling. AlphaFold3 proposed a diffusion based generative model as the structure module instead of IPA in AlphaFold2 to model protein/nucleic acid/ligand/ion/modified residue in one model. From MSA-guided geometry attention to transformer based protein prediction, we are now heading towards the multimodal foundation model based on language, equivariant geometry, and diffusion-based 3D coordinate generation.

The release of AlphaFold2 (post 2020 CASP14 assessment, Nature, 2021) was a turning point for protein structure prediction. It employed a series of Evoformer modules that continually cycled information between residue pair representation and multi-sequence alignment (MSA) representation through attention and outer product updates. These representations were mapped to 3D coordinates using a structure module which relied on invariant point attention (IPA). It combined geometric reasoning and evolution information from sequence with the recycling of intermediate prediction, delivering a median of GDT-TS score of 92.4 in CASP14 (median GDT-TS score for the challenging free modeling targets is 87.0). IPA was a game-changer as the attention mechanism acted upon learned 3D points, but was invariant to global translation and rotation. ([Jumper et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2))

New architectures have continued this attention-focused approach. For example, RoseTTAFold (University of Washington, Science, 2021) employed a three-track network which jointly operates on 1D (sequence/MSA) features, 2D (residue pair) information, and 3D coordinates. Information flow between representations was mediated by attention mechanisms, graph-transformer type operations, and SE(3) equivariant layers. The end-to-end implementation predicted backbone coordinates for proteins <400 residues in ~10 minutes on an RTX 2080 GPU. ([Baek et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj8754)) Meanwhile, protein language models have approached structure prediction as an emergent property of representation learning at the sequence scale. For example, Meta's ESM-2 and ESMFold structure predictions from single sequence representation (using Transformer language model embeddings) avoid the computational cost of using explicit MSAs. (Published in Science 2023) The ESMFold model powers the ESM Metagenomic Atlas (over 617 million protein predictions) but tends to be less accurate than AlphaFold2. ([Lin et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ade2574))

The latest release of AlphaFold3 (Nature, 2024) expands this from protein folding to biomolecular interaction modeling. It substitutes the AlphaFold2 IPA-based structure module with a generative (diffusion-based) architecture which can model proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, ions, and modified residues all in one. Transformer-based protein prediction has thus shifted from geometric attention (MSA conditioned) to multimodal foundation models that combine language representations, equivariant geometry, and diffusion-based 3D coordinate generation.

paper_section_03_glm.text:
Results
The power conversion efficiency (PCE) of methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) perovskite precursor solution is found to be statistically significantly improved upon the addition of cesium bromide (CsBr). The champion devices made with 5 mol% CsBr showed 19.4% PCE, while undoped control devices showed 18.1% PCE, representing 7.2% absolute relative yield (1.3% absolute PCE gain). The improvement was observed in three different batches of fabrication made during March to May 2024. The champion PCE of the devices reached 19.1%-19.6% for CsBr-doped devices vs. 17.8%-18.3% for the control devices.
The AM 1.5G (100 mW cm -2 ) current density voltage (J-V) measurements demonstrated that the open-circuit voltage (V OC ) was the main contributor to the efficiency improvement, with values of 1.12 ± 0.02 V for CsBr-doped devices and 1.06 ± 0.03 V for control devices (n = 24 for each condition, p < 0.001, two tailed t-test). The short-circuit current density (J SC ) was slightly increased from 22.4 ± 0.6 mA cm -2 to 22.9 ± 0.5 mA cm -2 . However, the fill factor (FF) was statistically identical (FF = 0.74 ± 0.02 for both groups). Adding CsBr reduced the hysteresis index from 8.3% to 4.1%, which is attributed to suppressed ion migration. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) of the CsBr-doped perovskite films exhibited 0.14° 2θ shift toward higher angle for (110) peak and the disappearance of the PbI 2 peak at 12.7° angle, suggesting A-site partial substitution of Cs + and enhanced phase purity. The larger grain size (mean size 412 ± 95 nm for CsBr-doped devices vs. 287 ± 78 nm for control) in the CsBr-doped films based on scanning electron microscopy (SEM) results correlated to the reduced density of trap states (from 1.8 × 10 16 to 1.1 × 10 16 cm -3 ) as determined using space-charge-limited current analysis. The CsBr-doped devices maintained 88% of initial PCE after 500 hours of constant illumination at 65 °C, while the control devices maintained 74% of initial PCE. However, the devices doped with CsBr concentrations higher than 5 mol% (10 and 15 mol% CsBr were investigated) exhibited phase segregation and poorer performance (PCE was 17.2% and 15.9%, respectively). Therefore, the optimized CsBr doping level was found to be 5 mol% in the studied concentration range.

Results

Integration of cesium bromide (CsBr) into methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) perovskite precursor solution was found to yield a statistically significant boost in power conversion efficiency (PCE). The champion 5 mol% CsBr-doped devices exhibited a PCE of 19.4%, compared to 18.1% for undoped control devices, for a relative yield gain of 7.2% (absolute yield gain 1.3%) over three independent batches of fabrication (March-May 2024). Champion devices in CsBr-doped films showed a PCE range of 19.1-19.6%, compared to 17.8-18.3% in control films.

Current density-voltage (J-V) scans conducted under AM 1.5G (100 mW cm(-2)) revealed that the efficiency boost is mainly due to an increase of the open-circuit voltage (V OC): 1.12 +/- 0.02 V for doped devices vs 1.06 +/- 0.03 V for control devices, n = 24 devices in each group, p < 0.001 (two-tailed t-test). A slight increase in short circuit current density (J SC) from 22.4 +/- 0.6 to 22.9 +/- 0.5 mA cm(-2) was also observed. Fill factor was statistically not affected (FF 0.74 +/- 0.02 in both cases). Hysteresis indices are lower with CsBr integration: 8.3% to 4.1%, reflecting lower ion migration.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) of doped films showed that the (110) peak has shifted by 0.14 degrees to higher 2 theta and the PbI2 peak at 12.7 degrees disappeared, suggesting Cs+ partial substitution in the A-site and higher phase purity. Scanning electron microscopy indicated larger grains, with an average size of 412 +/- 95 nm compared to 287 +/- 78 nm for control films. This correlates with lower trap state density (from 1.8E16 to 1.1E16 cm(-3) as obtained through space-charge-limited current analysis.

Under continuous illumination and 65 degrees C, 88% of the initial PCE remained in doped devices after 500 h of exposure, compared to 74% for control devices. Doping above 5 mol% (10 and 15 mol%) showed phase segregation and reduced performance (PCE 17.2%, 15.9%, respectively), with 5 mol% CsBr showing the optimal value in the investigated composition range.

paper_section_05_sonnet.text:
Prediction of 90-day readmission to hospital using gradient boosting and longitudinal EHR data from the MIMIC-IV

Background: 90-day, unplanned hospital readmissions are important and expensive outcomes. Most predictive modeling for 90-day readmissions has been centered around 30-day readmissions which are mandated for CMS reporting.

Methods: We extracted 51238 adult inpatient admissions (2008-2019) from MIMIC-IV v2.2 (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston MA), excluding in-hospital deaths or discharge to hospice, for a total of 46904 index admissions. 90-day readmissions were defined as any additional inpatient encounters within 90 days of the discharge (positive rate: 21.4%, n=10038). We created 187 features including demographics, Elixhauser comorbidity index, admission severity (SOFA, SAPS-II), lab values over the last 48 hours of hospitalization, medications at discharge, length of stay and prior encounters (ED visits or admissions in last 12 months). Subjects were split by unique ID (70/15/15 for train/validation/test) to avoid leakage between encounters. We trained and tested XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost classifiers and optimized hyperparameters (5-fold cross-validated Bayesian optimization, 100 trials, Optuna from training set) using 5-fold cross-validation on training set with early stopping on AUROC on validation set.

Results: LightGBM was our top performing model for the held-out test set (AUROC 0.762, 95% CI: 0.748-0.776; AUPRC:0.451; Brier: 0.142). It outperformed a logistic regression model (AUROC:0.681) and slightly outperformed XGBoost (AUROC: 0.754) and Catboost (AUROC:0.758). Top features identified using SHAP included previous admission counts in 12 months, discharge Hb, Elixhauser comorbidity score and discharge disposition (skilled nursing vs. home). The model was well-calibrated across different risk deciles (HL p=0.34). Using a threshold that identifies the top 20% risk, our model had a sensitivity of 58.3% to detect true readmissions and had a positive predictive value of 47.1%.

Conclusions: Gradient boosting models for 90-day readmission using commonly collected features in MIMIC-IV data have good predictive performance for clinically important risk of 90-day readmissions, with potential applications to increase the horizon of discharge planning activities beyond 30-days. Results need to be validated in non-ICU-weighted datasets.

Prediction of 90-day hospital readmission using gradient boosting with longitudinal electronic health record data from MIMIC-IV

Background: The risk of unplanned hospital readmission within 90 days post-discharge is both an expensive and important clinical outcome but most prediction models have focused on 30-day readmissions that are required for CMS reporting and less focus has been placed on prediction for longer time periods.

Methods: In MIMIC-IV v2.2 (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA), we extracted data for 51,238 adult inpatient admissions (2008-2019). We excluded in-hospital death and hospice discharges leaving 46,904 eligible index admissions. We defined 90-day readmission as subsequent hospital admissions within 90 days post-discharge. (positivity rate: 21.4%, n=10,038). We created 187 features including demographics, Elixhauser comorbidity indices, admission severity (SOFA, SAPS-II), laboratory data within the last 48 hours prior to discharge, total medication discharge counts, length of stay, prior utilization (ED visits and hospital admissions within last 12 months). Data was partitioned based on unique subject ID (70/15/15 train/validation/test) to avoid encounter data leakage. We developed XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost classifiers. Hyperparameter tuning was performed with 5-fold cross-validation Bayesian optimization (100 trials, Optuna) of training data using early stopping based on AUROC in validation data.

Results: Using LightGBM, we found the highest out-of-sample predictive performance (AUROC 0.762 95% CI 0.748-0.776, AUPRC:0.451, Brier Score:0.142) compared to logistic regression (AUROC:0.681). Slightly better than XGBoost (AUROC: 0.754) and CatBoost (AUROC: 0.758). The 4 features most important from SHAP analysis were: Prior 12-months admissions count, Hemoglobin at discharge, Elixhauser comorbidity score, Disposition at discharge (skilled nursing vs home). We found strong calibration performance across deciles (HL p=0.34). Our model detected the top 20% highest risk patients using a threshold, with 58.3% (sensitivity) of true readmissions and PPV of 47.1%.

Conclusions: Gradient boosting classifiers of routinely available MIMIC-IV data can demonstrate clinically relevant separation in 90-day risk of readmission, and may facilitate 90-day planning interventions beyond the traditional focus on 30 days, subject to external validation on non-ICU weighted data sets.

paper_section_07_luna.text:
In October 2023-August 2024, we randomly assigned drip-irrigation information and price subsidies (50% or 75% voucher value) in a field experiment with 1,150 vegetable growing smallholder farmers in Makueni and Kitui counties, Kenya. We selected households from village-level agricultural lists and pre-screened households based on landholdings of 0.1-2.0 hectares, rainfed-and/or-manual irrigation as the primary irrigation method, and no current use of drip irrigation. After baseline surveys, farmers were stratified by county and baseline irrigated area, and then randomly assigned to (1) receive information only (n = 383), (2) receive information and a 50% voucher for a drip-irrigation kit (n = 384), or (3) receive information and a 75% voucher (n = 383).

All treatment households received a two-hour demonstration, led by local trained agricultural extension officers, in November 2023. The demonstrations focused on how to install, maintain, and conserve water with drip irrigation, including expected water savings and crop-specific usage rates (illustrated with a 0.1-hectare demonstration plot). The vouchers could be redeemed at participating agro-dealers in Makueni and Kitui counties through February 29, 2024. Drip kits contained a 500-liter storage tank, low-pressure filter, 100 meters of lateral line, connectors, and estimated 0.1 hectare irrigation capacity. The information-only group received the same technical information, without any price discount.

Trained and treatment-blinded enumerators completed baseline, four-month post-voucher-expiration, and endline-main-season (2024) in-person surveys. The main outcome of interest is drip adoption (installation and use on ≥0.05 hectares in the last 30 days before endline survey). Additional outcomes of interest are the amount of land put under production, frequency of irrigation, input costs, crop yields, farm income, water usage, and perceived labor demands. We collect crop production data from farmer records and random crop-cutting plots. We use ordinary least squares to estimate intention-to-treat effects. We include county fixed effects and pre-specified baseline controls, and cluster standard errors by village.

We implemented a field experiment between October 2023 and August 2024 with 1,150 smallholder vegetable farmers in Makueni and Kitui counties, Kenya. Using agricultural registers at the village level, we selected and screened eligible households that grew crops on 0.1-2.0 ha and were mainly rain-fed or manually irrigated. Households that currently did not use drip irrigation were then randomly assigned (by county, baseline irrigated area) to information-only (n = 383), information and 50% voucher to purchase a drip irrigation kit (n = 384), or information and 75% voucher (n = 383) groups.

All treatment households received a 2-hour demonstration by locally trained agricultural extension agents in November 2023 on drip irrigation installation and maintenance, potential water savings, and crop-specific rates to be applied on a 0.1 ha demonstration plot. Vouchers could be redeemed with participating agro-dealers in Makueni and Kitui until February 29, 2024. Each kit came with a 500-liter storage tank, a low-pressure filter, 100 meters of lateral tubing, connectors, and can reportedly irrigate 0.1 ha. For information-only farmers, all technical information was delivered without any price reduction.

Unblinded enumerators collected data in-person at baseline, 4 months after the voucher expiry and at the end of the main 2024 growing season. Our main outcome was drip irrigation adoption, where the drip irrigation system was installed and used on at least 0.05 ha during the last 30 days before the endline survey. We measured several secondary outcomes including the area under production, irrigation frequency, input costs, vegetable production, farm income, water consumption, and reported labor demand. We captured crop production through farmer records and randomly selected crop cutting plots. Using ordinary least squares with county fixed effects, pre-specified baseline covariates, and clustered standard errors at the village level, we estimated the intention-to-treat effects.

paper_section_09_glm.text:
DISCUSSION

Our 8 week high fat diet (HFD; 60% kcal from fat) resulted in profound and replicable changes to murine cecal microbiome taxa, specifically at the genus level, in line with previous reports (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Turnbaugh et al., 2006) and with added quantitative understanding of effect sizes and individual variance. Within our C57BL/6J group (n = 12 HFD, n = 11 chow controls), the most reliable change was a 14.3 fold increase in Bilophila (log 2 fold change = 3.84, q 0.002 adjusted, DESeq2 with Benjamini-Hochberg correction), which has bile tolerance in line with a mechanistic basis for the increase in tauroconjugated bile acids with dietary fat intake. This would support the notion that sulfide production by Bilophila is associated with impairment of the intestinal barrier.

On the other hand, we saw a significant decrease in the mucin-breaking bacterium Akkermansia (log2FC =-2.61, q = 0.008), which has been shown multiple times to be beneficial for metabolic outcomes in both rodents and humans. The role of Akkermansia loss being part of, or causing, HFD metabolic endotoxemia is unclear but our results indicate that loss of Akkermansia occurred before overt rise in fasting glucose levels (by 2 weeks on average) in the animals suggesting a causal direction but cannot be definitively proven with this approach.

It should be noted that the change in Lactobacillus level (log2FC =-1.78, q = 0.03) is due largely to three animals and removing them as outliers in sensitivity analyses changed the effect to non-significant (q = 0.11). Furthermore, the seemingly increased levels of Clostridium XIVa (log 2 fold change = 1.92, q = 0.048) were borderline significant and could be an artefact of normalizing the composition and not an actual change in level. Relative count data is limited in this regard and we accounted partially for it by using ANCOM-BC for confirmation.

Alpha diversity (mean Shannon index) was reduced on average in the HFD group (3.12 vs. 3.58, p-value 0.009 Wilcoxon) and beta-diversity separated the two groups on PCo1 (PERMANOVA R2 = 0.19, p-value 0.001) showing that the perturbation in the microbiota by diet goes beyond individual taxa. Whether or not this can be reversed by normalizing the diet and what are the recovered taxa that reflect restoration of insulin sensitivity are the topics of ongoing research in our lab.

Discussion.

High fat diet (HFD, 60%kcal from fat) for 8 weeks led to significant and generally reproducible genus-level changes in the murine cecal microbiota (as previously described in Bäckhed et al. (2004); Turnbaugh et al. (2006)) with the added benefit of quantification for effects size and inter-individual variance. The strongest effect in our C57BL/6J animals (n = 12 for HFD, n = 11 chow control animals) was the 14.3 fold increase (log2FC: 3.84) in Bilophila (adjusted q = 0.002, DESeq2 with BH adjustment) which mechanistically makes sense because of the physiology of the organism's bile tolerance as it relates to high tauroconjugated bile acids in response to dietary fat. These changes agree with the suggested role of sulfide from Bilophila on impaired intestinal barrier function.

We also found a significant decrease in Akkermansia (log2FC:-2.61, q = 0.008) which is a mucin-degrading genus that has been linked repeatedly with health and metabolic status in mice and humans. The role of loss of Akkermansia as driver or passenger for metabolic endotoxemia induced by HFD is not clear yet. We found that the loss of Akkermansia was evident 2 weeks or so before there was an elevation of fasting glucose which suggests a causal relation but cannot be proved in this study.

The decrease of Lactobacillus (log2FC:-1.78, q = 0.03) was mostly driven by three animals. When we removed these outliers, the effect was not significant (q = 0.11). The possible increase in Clostridium XIVa (log2FC: 1.92, q = 0.048) was near significant and could be an artifact of normalization for composition. This is a limitation of using relative count data which we tried to overcome somewhat by using ANCOM-BC as a confirmatory approach.

We found modest decreases in alpha diversity (mean Shannon index: 3.12 vs 3.58, p-value Wilcoxon = 0.009) and differences in beta diversity between groups (on PCo1, PERMANOVA r2 = 0.19, p-value = 0.001) which suggests the dietary intervention caused changes in composition beyond individual taxonomic changes. It is unclear whether these changes can be reversed after diet normalization and which genera respond to recovery of insulin sensitivity. These questions are ongoing in our laboratory.

paper_section_11_sonnet.text:
Heterogeneous treatment effects have gone from a robustness test to a primary focus of research in labor economics. Bayesian estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects appears to be a very natural way to estimate them in sparse and high-dimensional settings common to policy research. When the goal is to produce credible estimates of uncertainty about the true effect within particular subgroups in a population, classical approaches often lack the flexibility to provide informative results. Bayesian hierarchical models allow for partial pooling across sub-groups, combining information to shrink noisy effects within sub-groups towards more stable population-wide effects. This line of thinking began with Rubin (1981) writing about parallel experiments and was first applied to empirical labor economics with some success by looking at job training programs. A key application was to re-analyze data from the National Supported Work Demonstration originally examined by LaLonde (1986).

Over the past 10 years there has been increasing interest in Bayesian methods for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects. Two key recent developments: First, the addition of Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (Chipman, George, and McCulloch, 2010) to causal analysis settings. Most notably, Hill (2011) introduced the Bayesian Causal Forest model, which allows for nonparametric estimation of conditional average treatment effects with flexible flexibility while providing complete information about the uncertainty of the posterior distributions. Second, recent applications to large datasets of administrative data - for example, Angrist and Pallais et al. studies of job search assistance programs or studies using Danish/German social insurance data for population sizes over a million individuals - have shown that there are significant gains from using Bayesian shrinkage methods (compared to just estimating effects in individual sub-groups) when we have heterogeneous treatment effects measured within hundreds of groups defined by age, education, local labor market.

A related line of work considers Bayesian estimation of instruments and regression discontinuity designs in situations where instruments may be weak as is often the case in the minimum wage and unemployment insurance extension literature. For example, Kline and Tartari (2016) look at welfare to work experiments using Bayesian methods. And, Meager (2019) has a meta-analysis of microcredit trials. Hierarchical priors can help resolve apparently conflicting results across sites.

This paper discusses these ideas, compares the methods against each other using simulated labor market data (based on the 2019 Current Population Survey), and provides recommendations for applied researchers about when to use BART-based methods, Gaussian process methods, or shrinkage prior methods.

Bayesian approaches to the estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects have become more prominent in labor economics from both a robustness and primary interest perspective. They are particularly successful for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects when data is sparse and high-dimensional as is often the case with policy evaluations. In particular, Bayesian hierarchical models can address the problem classical methods have when reporting uncertainty for estimates of treatment effects within subgroups. This is because Bayesian methods can partially pool subgroups to borrow strength from the patterns across subgroups, "shrinking" noisy subgroup estimates towards robust patterns of the population as a whole. This concept can be traced back to Rubin's (1981) work on parallel experiments. The empirical implementation of Bayesian estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects in labor economics received some of its earliest implementations with the evaluation of job training programs. Examples include re-analysis of data from the National Supported Work Demonstration first analyzed by LaLonde (1986).

In the last decade, two major developments have contributed to greater adoption. First, the use of Bayesian additive regression trees (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010) as part of a causal inference framework such as Hill's (2011) Bayesian Causal Forest allow for flexible nonparametric estimation of conditional average treatment effects with full uncertainty (posterior) quantification. Second, the growing use of Bayesian models in applied settings for big administrative data such as Angrist, Pallais, and others' analysis of job search assistance and studies with Danish or German social insurance data for over a million workers show how shrinkage (pooling) of Bayesian methods can dominate non-pooled (naive) subgroup estimates when treatment effects differ for hundreds of subgroups defined by age, education, and local labor market conditions.

Relatedly, Bayesian methods for instrumental variables and regression discontinuity designs have also been explored. They help solve common issues of weak instruments particularly in the minimum wage and extended unemployment insurance literature. For example, Kline and Tartari's (2016) use of Bayesian methods for welfare to work experiments and Meager's (2019) meta-analysis of microcredit experiments show how we can use hierarchical priors to resolve seemingly conflicting results across sites.

This paper provides a brief review of this methodology, their empirical comparison to simulated labor market data based on the 2019 Current Population Survey, and some guidance for applied researchers who want to select among BART, Gaussian process, and shrinkage priors estimators.

paper_section_13_luna.text:
We found a robust preference for point-light walker displays based on eye-tracking data from 64 healthy infants studied at the University of Washington Infant Learning and Development Laboratory, Seattle, March-August, 2024. Subjects included 32 female and 32 male infants, ages 5-7 months (mean age 6.1 months, SD = 0.7). In each trial (N = 24 trials per infant) infants viewed upright and inverted point-light walker or phase scrambled motion control (matching dot array) stimuli. Only trials with >50% of valid data from the 2 s presentation time (N = 91.8% valid) included.

Infants looked more at upright (M = 61.7%, 95%CI [59.2-64.2]) versus their control stimulus in the pair, t(63) = 5.84, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.73. Also, more of the time infants fixated upright walkers first (68% of trials) compared to chance, χ2 (1) = 13.76, p < .001. In contrast, we didn't see reliable above chance looking for inverted (M = 51.9%) t(63) = 1.21, p = .23 or scrambled (M = 49.8%) t(63) = -0.18, p = .86 displays. A linear mixed-effects model with infants age, sex, trial type and trial number included a significant main effect of display type, F(2, 126) = 12.47, p < .001. Posthoc comparisons showed more looking at upright versus inverted (mean diff. = 9.8% pts, p = .002) and scrambled (mean diff. = 11.9% pts, p < .001). Neither age nor sex moderated preference. These results indicate that infants as young as 5-7 months are sensitive to the overall coherent kinematic information that is unique to human biological motion -as opposed to simple local dot motion or the overall stimulus energy.

In 64 healthy infants (32 males; 32 females, age 5–7 months; mean age = 6.1 months; SD = 0.7) tested in the University of Washington Infant Learning and Development Laboratory in Seattle between March and August 2024 eye-tracking results revealed a consistent bias for point light walkers displays. We presented 24 trials of either a point light upright walker, inverted walker, or phase scrambled motion control presented in conjunction with a visually matched dot array of static dots to each infant. Trials were included if infants had a valid eye-tracking record in >50% of the 2-s trial. Overall, 91.8% of samples were valid.

Infants spent more of their total looking time (M = 61.7%, 95% CI [59.2, 64.2]) looking at the upright walker displays than they did on the corresponding control stimulus t(63) = 5.84, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 0.73. The bias for the upright walker display was reflected in the first fixation data, with infants looking at the upright walker first on 68% of the trials, significantly more than chance, χ²(1) = 13.76, p < .001. Looking at the inverted walker display (M = 51.9%) and at the scrambled display (M = 49.8%) was not significantly greater than chance, t(63) = 1.21, p = .23 and t(63) = −0.18, p = .86 respectively. A linear mixed-effects model regressing infant age, sex, display type, and trial number indicated a significant main effect of display type, F(2, 126) = 12.47, p < .001. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons indicated that more looking time was spent at the upright walker display than at either the inverted walkers (mean difference = 9.8 percentage points, p = .002) or scrambled displays (mean difference = 11.9 percentage points, p < .001). Neither age nor sex had a significant moderating effect on the bias. This indicates that 5–7 month old infants are tuned to the coherent kinematic properties of the human biological motion, rather than just to individual point motion or to the energy of the display.

paper_section_15_glm.text:
Abstract
Mindfulness training has been suggested as a cost-effective strategy to improve working memory capacity (WMC), although individual studies show inconsistent and variable effects. The aim of this meta-analysis is to estimate the overall effect of mindfulness-based interventions on WMC and explore moderators of the effectiveness of such training. We conducted a database search in PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus between January 2000 and March 2024, and selected 38 relevant studies (k = 41 independent samples; N = 3,247) that compared mindfulness training against active or non-active controls and measured WMC using behavioral tests (e.g., complex span tasks, n-back, Operation Span). A random effect model showed a small-to-moderate overall effect (Hedges'g = 0.38, 95%CI [0.24, 0.52]; p < .001) with significant heterogeneity (Q = 96.4; I 2 = 58.6%). Moderators showed that the effect was greater with longer interventions (≥8 weeks vs. <8 weeks; β = 0.21; p = .012), when the intervention was instructor-led compared to app-based training (g = 0.46 vs. g = 0.22; p = .031), and for populations with higher levels of stress such as students in exam period or military personnel pre-deployment. We did not find significant differences in the effect according to age groups, type of meditation (focused attention vs. open monitoring) and year of publication. Risk of bias analysis (RoB 2) showed 12 studies as low, 21 with some concerns, and 5 as high risk. Egger's regression test showed potential small study effects (p = .048) and trim-and-fill procedure reduced the corrected estimate (g = 0.31). Sensitivity analyses showed that the overall effect is robust to outliers and type of control. These results indicate that mindfulness training with proper structure, ideally eight or more weeks and led by a live instructor, produces a small but significant effect on WMC. These results should be considered in the context of heterogeneity and likely publication bias. We discuss the implications for research on cognitive training and offer recommendations for future randomized trials (preregistration, active controls, and larger sample).

Keywords
mindfulness, working memory, meta-analysis, cognitive training, intervention.

Abstract
Mindfulness practice is suggested as a low-cost intervention for improving working memory capacity (WMC), but individual studies show inconsistent and diverse effect sizes. The aim of the present meta-analysis is to calculate the net effect of mindfulness-based interventions on WMC, and to examine factors that moderate the effectiveness of the intervention. A literature search was conducted on PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus (January 2000 to March 2024), resulting in 38 studies (k = 41 independent samples, N = 3,247 participants) that compared mindfulness interventions with active or non-active control groups, and measured WMC using behavioural tasks (e.g., complex span, n-back, Operation Span). Overall, there was a small to medium effect size (Hedges' g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.24, 0.52], p < .001) in the random-effect model with significant heterogeneity (Q = 96.4, I 2 = 58.6%). Further analyses showed the intervention has a greater effect with longer intervention duration (≥ 8 weeks vs < 8 weeks, β = 0.21, p = .012), with instructor-led interventions compared to app-based ones (g = 0.46 vs 0.22, p = .031), and in participants with high pre-intervention stress levels (e.g., students during examinations, military personnel pre-deployment). However, the effects were not significantly different between age groups, meditation types (focused attention vs open monitoring), or years of publication. According to RoB 2, 12 studies were rated low risk, 21 studies were rated some concerns, and 5 studies were rated high risk. Egger's regression test indicated potential small-study effects (p = .048), with the corrected estimate using trim-and-fill analysis resulting in a reduced effect size (g = 0.31). Sensitivity analyses revealed no outlier or control group-related threats to the overall effect. Our findings support that structured mindfulness practice-especially over 8 or more weeks in live instructor-led interventions-improves WMC moderately and reliably. Heterogeneity and potential publication bias are important to consider. Implications for cognitive training research are discussed. Recommendations for future randomized trials are provided, including preregistration, appropriate active control groups, and larger sample sizes.

Keywords: mindfulness, working memory, meta-analysis, cognitive training, intervention

Methods
To estimate the employment impacts of the 2014 Seattle minimum wage ordinance, we employ a difference-in-differences analysis relative to a synthetic control group (generated from nearby King County ZIP codes and similar labor markets in Washington State outside of the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue metropolitan statistical area). The Seattle minimum wage ordinance was approved by the Seattle City Council on June 2, 2014. It set phased-in minimum wage increases starting April 1, 2015 from the state minimum ($9.47) to $11.00 for large employers (500+ workers) with further gradual increases to $15.00 for large employers (500+ workers) without medical benefits by January 1, 2017 and for small employers by January 1, 2019.

Our main data source is quarterly Unemployment Insurance (UI) wage data from the Washington State Employment Security Department (2005Q1-2018Q4) for hourly employees working in food service (NAICS 722) and retail trade (NAICS 44-45), which is the industry where minimum-wage-bound jobs are most concentrated. We use a balanced panel of 2,847 establishments that are continuously observed throughout our data period. To find comparison establishments, we match our establishments with propensity score weights using pre-period (2005Q1-2014Q2) trends in hours, headcount, and average hourly wages.

Our baseline specification is:

Y_it = β(Seattle_i× Post_t) + α_i + γ_t + X_it′δ + ε_it

where Y_it is log employment or log hours at establishment i in quarter t; Seattle_i is a dummy for treated establishments; Post_t is a dummy for quarters after April 2015; α_i and γ_t are establishment and quarter fixed effects, respectively; and X_it includes establishment size and a dummy for single-site establishments. Standard errors are ZIP-code-clustered (94 clusters). To check the assumption of parallel trends, we calculate event-study coefficients separately for each quarter in the period from 2013Q1 to 2018Q4, where 2015Q1 is the omitted reference period. In addition, we present our results broken down by the different minimum wage bins ($9.47-$11, $11-$13, >$13) to account for the different biting of the minimum wage.

Methods
We apply a difference-in-differences method to estimate the employment impact of the 2014 Seattle minimum wage ordinance using synthetic control based on surrounding King County ZIP codes and similar Washington State labor markets outside of the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue metro area as the control group. Seattle City Council adopted the minimum wage ordinance on June 2, 2014, which incrementally increases the minimum wage from April 1, 2015, upwards from Washington state minimum of $9.47 to $11.00 for large (500+) employers, and subsequently to $15.00 by Jan. 1, 2017 for large employers (without medical benefits) and by Jan. 1, 2019 for small employers.

The main data set is the Washington State Employment Security Department's quarterly Unemployment Insurance (UI) wage data for 2005Q1-2018Q4, where we focus on hourly workers in food service (NAICS 722) and retail trade (NAICS 44-45) as these sectors have the highest concentration of minimum wage-bound employment. We create a balanced panel of 2,847 establishments who are present in the sample period. We link these to comparison establishments through propensity score weighting (for trends in hours, headcount, and average wage per hour in the pre-period 2005Q1-2014Q2).

The baseline empirical model is the following:

Y_it = β(Seattle_i * Post_t) + α_i + γ_t + X_it * δ + ε_it

where Y_it is the log of employment or log of hours at establishment i in quarter t. Seattle_i is an indicator for treated establishment. Post_t is an indicator for post-April 2015 quarters. α_i is establishment fixed effect. γ_t is quarter fixed effect. X_it includes establishment size and indicator for single-site status. We cluster standard error by ZIP code (94 clusters). To test the parallel trends assumption, we show coefficients of event study estimation (separate for every quarter from 2013Q1 to 2018Q4. Omitted quarter is 2015Q1). We also present findings by different wage tier bin ($9.47-$11, $11-$13, >$13) to examine the heterogeneous bite in the wage distribution.

The unusual $T_g$ behavior of PMMA/PVDF blends is related to a large mobility mismatch between the components (the typical $T_g$ for PMMA is around 105--125 ${^\circ}$C, and for PVDF it is around $-50$ ${^\circ}$C). Nevertheless, DSC is often able to find only a single $T_g$, which depends on composition. So we can say that there is considerable mixing on molecular level, and that the reason for this is mainly the interactions between the carbonyl groups of PMMA and the segments containing hydrogen in PVDF.

The initial DSC studies (e.g. Roerdink et al., 1978) found a large range of compatible compositions for isotactic, atactic, and syndiotactic PMMA/PVDF blends. But the $T_g$ values were not linearly interpolated in a universal way. Instead, they were described by the Gordon--Taylor equation. $k$ (which depends on the composition and tacticity) was 2.38 (isotactic), 1.72 (atactic) and 1.39 (syndiotactic) for PMMA ([Roerdink et al., 1978](https://doi.org/10.1016/0032-3861(78)90034-4)).

At high PVDF levels this $T_g$ anomaly is enhanced by crystallization or local composition variations at the nanoscale, which can smear or move the $T_g$ transition. For example, Huang and Zhang (2004) found some signs of weak specific interactions (carbonyl stretching shift in IR spectrum), but they also found higher heterogeneity and opacity with higher PVDF level. Therefore, the presence of only one $T_g$ in DSC can be misleading and do not necessarily indicate full thermodynamic homogeneity. The dielectric relaxation spectroscopy studies of the 4:1 and 3:2 PMMA/PVDF blends (2020) found higher relaxation strength and conductivity, indicating a certain compositional inhomogeneity on a nanoscale level ([Gonçalves et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1080/00222348.2020.1847393)).

So, the $T_g$ anomaly in PMMA/PVDF blends is complex. It depends on specific interchain interactions, compositionally dependent free volume, possible crystallinity of PVDF, processing conditions, etc. For proper understanding it is better to use a combination of DSC with spectroscopy, DMA and dielectric measurements. It is not good to use $T_g$ by itself as a binary index of miscibility.

The anomalous glass transition of PMMA/PVDF blends arises due to the significant mobility mismatch between segments of PMMA (typically with Tg around 105-125 C) and PVDF (Tg around -50C). Surprisingly, DSC experiments tend to show a single composition dependent transition instead of two separate glass transitions, which implies a significant molecular level intermixing, largely due to the carbonyl interaction of PMMA with the hydrogen segments of PVDF. Early calorimetric studies (Roerdink et al. 1978) showed compatibility over a large composition range for isotatic, atactic and syndiotactic PMMA/PVDF blends, but the Tg values showed a non universal linear interpolations, but fitted the Gordon-Taylor equation with composition and tacticity dependent k-values of 2.38, 1.72 and 1.39 for isotatic, atactic, syndiotactic PMMA [Roerdink et al. 1978, https://doi.org/10.1016/0032-3861(78)90034-4].

The paradox increases further for high PVDF fraction where crystallization and nanoscale composition fluctuations may cause broadening or shifts in the transition. Huang and Zhang (2004) found evidence for weak specific interactions (shift in carbonyl stretch in the infrared spectrum) but increased heterogeneity and opacity with increasing PVDF. Therefore, DSC single transition should not be a priori taken as sign of thermodynamic homogeneity. Recent dielectric relaxation studies of 4:1 and 3:2 PMMA/PVDF blends (2020) have shown increase in relaxation strength and conductivity indicating nanoscale compositional heterogeneity [Gonçalves et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.1080/00222348.2020.1847393]. The strange Tg behavior stems from the interplay between specific interchain interactions, composition dependent free volume, crystallinity of PVDF and history of the process. Thus, Tg alone should not be used as a binary miscibility factor. The DSC results need to be supplemented by spectral studies, DMCs, dielectric studies to accurately assess the situation.

Introduction Dose selection is one of the most important and underoptimized decisions in the practice of oncology. Current dosing protocols for cytotoxic chemotherapy agents (eg, 5-fluorouracil, carboplatin, doxorubicin) were largely defined by population dose finding studies (typically dose fixed per BSA and protocol-mandated dose de-escalations for toxicity) in the 1980's-1990's. This "one size fits all" approach fails to account for the considerable intra-and inter-patient variability in pharmacokinetic parameters (sometimes >10x in drug clearance) that characterize cytotoxic chemotherapy. The clinical impact of suboptimal chemotherapy dosing has been described. Underdosing leads to suboptimal tumor control, while overdosing causes grade 3/4 neutropenia/neuropathy, and treatment discontinuation. For example, retrospective studies have shown that less than 30% of patients receive the (post hoc identified) optimally tolerated dose trajectory of FOLFOX chemotherapy in metastatic colorectal cancer.

The task of dosing is a sequential decision-making problem and reinforcement learning (RL) provides a principled way to think about these decisions. Each treatment cycle can be thought of as a Markov decision process in which the clinician receives a state (blood counts, toxicity grades, biomarkers, performance status), takes an action (dose level/timing/agent changes) and receives a reward (trade off between tumor response and accumulated toxicity). Proof of concept studies by Zhao et al (2011) showed that a fully observable RL agent (using simulated patient data) could be more effective than static protocols in a compartmental model of myelosuppression. Recent advances in offline RL techniques (eg, conservative Q-learning, behavior cloned policy constraints, doubly robust off policy evaluation) now allow us to leverage observational electronic health record data for learning without any dangerous online exploration in vulnerable patients. Recent 2022-2024 TempoRL and other dose optimization programs at institutions like MD Anderson, Duke have started to move these techniques to prospective assessment.

There are major challenges that stand between these retrospective RL benchmarks and implementable trial interventions, such as partially observable disease burden, non-stationarity of patient physiology across courses of treatment, conservative safety constraints, and regulatory considerations in light of FDA guidance for adaptive trial designs and AI/ML enabled software as medical device. In this paper, we provide a review of chemotherapy dosing adaptation framed as an RL problem, assessment of the strengths and limitations of prior methodological approaches, and a trial design (utilizing off-policy confidence bounds and clinician in the loop policy veto) which we argue is a necessary precursor to first in human assessment.

Introduction
Optimal chemotherapy dosing is one of the most important and least optimized decisions in oncology. For many cytotoxic agents (5-fluorouracil, carboplatin, doxorubicin, etc), currently used standard-of-care dosing schemes were first determined through population level dose-finding trials in the 1980's-1990's. These dosing schemes generally prescribe a fixed dose (e.g. normalized to body surface area) and mandate dose de-escalation based on toxicity. The "one-size-fits-all" approach to chemotherapy does not account for the large inter/intra-patient pharmacokinetic variability of cytotoxic treatments (often 10x drug clearance variability). The clinical consequences of this variability are well-known, including insufficient tumor control from under-dosing and grade 3/4 neutropenia, neuropathy, and treatment discontinuation from over-dosing. For example, retrospective analyses of FOLFOX use for metastatic colorectal cancer suggest that less than 30% of patients receive the estimated optimal tolerated dose trajectory (in post-hoc modeling).

Chemotherapy dosing is a prime example of a sequential decision problem, which is well-suited to a reinforcement learning (RL) framework. At each cycle of treatment the physician agent is in some state (e.g. blood counts, toxicity grades, biomarkers, performance status) and chooses an action (dose, timing, or agent change) and gets a reward based on the tumor response vs. accumulated toxicity tradeoff. Early proof-of-concept results by Zhao et al. (2011) showed that a RL agent (for a fully observable problem) could beat a fixed protocol approach for simulated patient data in a compartmental myelosuppression model. More recently, offline RL approaches (conservative Q-learning, behavior-cloned policy constraints, doubly robust off-policy evaluation) have allowed learning from observational electronic health record data, without the need for risky exploration in vulnerable populations. Recent (2022-2024) 2024TempoRL (and similar) dose optimization efforts at institutions like MD Anderson and Duke are starting to apply these techniques for potential prospective evaluation.

Despite the RL benchmark studies in a retrospective setting, there are substantial challenges to moving to trial interventions, including partial observability of disease load, non-stationarity of patient physiology throughout treatment, safety considerations with conservative constraints, and regulatory challenges (FDA guidance on adaptive trials, AI/ML as software medical device). This paper discusses the framing of adaptive chemotherapy dosing in an RL setting, assesses the methodological challenges and successes of the published RL approaches, and provides a proposed trial design (with off-policy confidence bounds, clinician-in-the-loop policy veto) as a pre-requisite to first-in-human evaluation.

Got laid off from teaching in August. 
 Here's what I learned in my first 60 days 
 On Aug 12 (2 days before inservice week began) I received a phone call from my principal at Jefferson Elementary informing me that my position was being "eliminated because of a decline in enrollment" 
 6 years of 4th grade teaching evaporated in a 4 minute phone call. 
 I'm not asking for sympathy. 
 Just giving you some insight into the last 2 months.  What an education it's been. 
 Wish someone had told me these things on day 1. 
 Unemployment paperwork is a second job. 
 Took me 3 weeks and 2 rejected applications to figure out that I entered my last day of work incorrectly. 
 Do it asap.  Triple check it. 
 1st check didn't arrive until September 19th 
 You possess more job skills from teaching than you realize but nobody else knows this. 
 I was sending out resumes for "training" jobs and "instructional design" jobs.  Never hearing anything. 
 As soon as I re-worded my resume to say "managed a team of 28 people.  6 hour daily presentations.  Performance data analysis" instead of "4th grade teacher", I've been on 4 interviews in 2 weeks. 
 Starting my new job Monday the 14th. 
 Customer success rep for a software company in CR. 
 Not teaching but $9K more than I was making at the school district. 
 Grieve.  It's weird. 
 I'm in the school supply aisle at Target on Aug 20th and I'm crying. 
 Didn't see that coming. 
 Embrace the weird. 
 People want to help. 
 You have to ask. 
 I had an ex-parent who heard I got laid off. 
 Hooked me up with the company I'm working for now. 
 Couldn't find that job on Indeed. 
 For those teachers who are still in the classroom and wondering about your jobs.... 
 Start working on your resume now. 
 Not after you get the phone call. 
 
 Questions in the comments?  Shoot away. 
 For the Jefferson crew - I miss you guys.

 AITA for ignoring them now.  Let the professionals deal with the suspicious courthouse bees?

I (accidentally) became the town's unofficial beekeeper in June 2021. 
 Swarm of bees on maple tree outside my house in Cedar Falls.  I contact the city.  I contact the fire department.  I contact three different pest control companies.  They all say the same thing: don't mess with it.  I post a picture on our local FB group.  Old school beekeeper (Dennis) comes out with cardboard box, bedsheet, and an attitude of someone who's defusing a bomb. 
 We're able to put most of them in the box.  Hundreds of bees remain.  Dennis says 'probably gone in the morning'.  Nope.  Moved into my porch ceiling. 
 For the next two weeks, my neighbors are messaging me.  'Bees in the chimney on Oak St.'  'Bees in the mailbox on Franklin Ave.'  'Bees hanging from the playground fence by Lincoln Elementary.'  Apparently, I'm the expert here. 
 I'm not.  I've watched like 4 youtube videos. 
 So I buy a veil.  Borrow a smoker from Dennis.  Start contacting actual beekeepers.  Help organize removal of 11 swarms by August.  (One in the ceiling of our town library.  Librarian handed me a thank you card from the entire staff.  My 7 year old daughter starts calling me the 'bee lady'.  I'm a dude named Mark.) 
 Weirdest thing is people still reach out.  Got a voicemail last month:  'Suspicious hum near the courthouse.' 
 I'm not a beekeeper.  I've never had a hive.  Just happened to pick up the phone in 2021. 
 AITA for just not responding and letting the professionals take care of the suspicious courthouse bees?

I just returned from Portugal (3/3-3/12). I did the entire 10 day trip on $1200 or less (with flights).  So I flew round trip from Boston to Lisbon on TAP.  I paid $386.  I booked this 4 months ahead. 
 
 So my total was $1,176: 
 - Flights: $386 
 - Accommodations: $278 
 - Food: $214 
 - Train/Bus/Local transportation: $126 
 - Activities: $98 
 - Misc: $74 
 
 First 4 nights I stayed in Lisbon at Goodmorning Solo Traveller Hostel ($27/night). 
 Then train to Porto and stayed at Cats Hostel for 3 nights ($29/night). 
 Finally I stayed in Lagos for 2 nights in a simple guesthouse ($42/night).  The only night I splurged on accommodations was my last night.  The place was near Lisbon Airport and it was $58.  But it was because my flight was at 7:10am 
 
 For food, it was mostly bifana, pastel de nata, sandwiches from the supermarket, and daily menus (10€-14€).  The best food was at this tiny place in Porto called O Gaveto.  I had grilled sardines and potatoes and it was €13.  I did a group tour to Douro Valley (cost €22).  Sintra day trip train and bus (€18). 
 
  I saved so much money by just having my backpack and walking around and not taking taxis.  I was walking almost 20,000 steps a day.  Worst part was trying to see everything (Lisbon, Sintra, Porto, Lagos).  It was very tiring to have all of these travel days (like the 6 hr train ride from Porto to Lagos). 
 
 But I got to see Belém tower, hiked 7 Hanging Valleys trail, saw Livraria Lello, watched the sunset at Cabo da Roca, etc. 
 
 Is anyone else successful with traveling cheap in Portugal?  Or was I just lucky with the flights?

1 year / 15k miles with a 2023 model Y.. honest review (fucking $600 headache) 
 
 Got my model Y LR in march of 2023 from the delivery center in Costa Mesa CA. figured I'd post up an honest review (not a honeymoon review) at the 1 year mark. 
 
 POSITIVE 
  still always makes me smile with the acceleration.  Coming from a 2018 Honda CR-V it's night and day. 
  Costs me ~$11 to fully charge on my home 240V outlet. vs $70+ at the gas pump 
  supercharger network is amazing.  Went to phoenix in jan.. never worried about range 
  on the 5 freeway and traffic.. autopilot is a godsend 
  
 ANNOYING 
  Rear driver door still has some panel gaps visible. 
  Wipers still kind of do their own thing sometimes. 
  sentry mode definitely has an impact on battery drain 
  Can't fucking believe there's no physical blind spot indicator.  Biggest complaint by far. 
  had a phantom brake issue twice on the I-10.  Both times were pretty scary. 
  
 $600 repair 
  in november, my touchscreen began randomly rebooting while driving.  Went to costa mesa service center.  had it for 4 days.  issue is the MCU4 connector is bad. 
  Covered?  NOPE.  apparently because i had a aftermarket dashcam installed at a third party shop in september.  they claimed voltage interference. 
  $612 out of pocket.  maybe true.  maybe convenient excuse.  will never know 
  
 Verdict:  8/10.  The driving experience and money savings are there.  Build quality / accountability for service is holding it back.  Would i buy again?  Probably.. but no aftermarket electronics

Report Date: Year 2, Q3 (July 1st - September 21st, 2026)
PI: Dr. Rachel Ostrander; Department of Materials Science, Purdue University.

Summary
Award "Scalable Synthesis of Anisotropic Nanocomposites for Low-Energy Thermal Regulation" Year 2 progress. Five milestones were planned for Year 2. Three have been successfully completed.

1. Reactor scale-up (completed May 2026): Successfully commissioned the 5L continuous flow reactor in the West Lafayette lab with 92% (40x batch run consistency, > 85% target) yield.

2. Anisotropic alignment protocol development (completed July 2026): Graduate student Wei Chen established magnetic field-guided alignment protocol with 0.87 OP value. (Published in Advanced Materials Interfaces, August 2026 issue)

3. Thermal conductivity benchmarking (completed September 15, 2026): Postdoc Dr. Amara Osei finished commercial benchmark tests (12 composites) at Argonne National Laboratory CNM facility. Confirmed 34% cross plane thermal conductivity drop compared to the isotropic baseline.

Milestone 4 (durability testing after 500 thermal cycles) - 60% completed. Full data completion expected Dec. 2026.
Milestone 5 (integration into prototype thermal barrier device) - not started. Received confirmation of device housing availability Jan 2027 from our device fabrication partner Sandia National Labs.

Expenditure: Out of the Year 2 budget ($580,000), $412,000 has been spent (71%). In line with the approved spending plan.

Personnel: One undergrad researcher added (Marcus Devine) June 2026. Supported by REU supplement.

Next report period: Complete Milestone 4 (cycling data) and Milestone 5 (device integration) prior to the Year 2 annual report (Due March 1st, 2027).

Grant Progress Report NSF Award #2145987 Period covered: Year 2, Q3 (July 1 - Sept 21, 2026)
PI: Dr. Rachel Ostrander, Department of Materials Science, Purdue University

Summary: In the second year of the award entitled "Scalable Synthesis of Anisotropic Nanocomposites for Low-Energy Thermal Regulation", we have been focused on achieving five milestones. Three milestones have been met to date.

1. We have completed the 5L reactor scale-up (milestone 1, completed May 2026). We commissioned our 5L continuous flow reactor in our lab in West Lafayette. 40 batch runs were performed, and we achieved 92% consistent yield. This is above our 85% threshold of yield consistency.

2. Anisotropic alignment protocol developed (milestone 2, completed July 2026). This work was completed by graduate student Wei Chen, who developed a magnetic field assisted alignment protocol. This work has 0.87 order parameter. It has been published in Advanced Materials Interfaces (Aug 2026 issue).

3. Thermal conductivity benchmarking (milestone 3, completed 15Sept2026). Postdoc Dr. Amara Osei has successfully benchmarked against 12 commercial composites at Argonne National Lab (CNM facility). We have demonstrated 34% reduction of cross plane thermal conductivity compared to the isotropic composite.

Progress of remaining milestones: Milestone 4 (durability testing under 500 thermal cycles) is 60% complete. All data is anticipated by Dec 2026. Milestone 5 (integrated into thermal barrier prototype device) has not yet begun. Our fabrication partner, Sandia National Labs has verified that they have the device housing available for Jan 2027.

The spend for this award (Year 2, $580K) has been $412K spent (71%), which is in line with our approved spend plan.

We have added one undergraduate researcher, Marcus Devine (June 2026). We are supporting this researcher using the REU supplement.

Next reporting period: Finish Milestone 4 cycling data. Start integrating into Milestone 5 device. We will be reporting these results in the year 2 annual report (due 3/1/2027).

Field Research Log: Bird Population Counts - Cedar Swamp
Week of May 6-15, 2024
Submitted by: Dana Whitfield - Field Technician - Northline Audubon Society

Summary of Activity
3 person team D. Whitfield, M. Okafor, and intern J. Reyes.  We counted birds on 10 consecutive days and conducted 40 point count surveys within the Cedar Swamp survey grid.  We were able to conduct surveys at all 8 established stations during the morning window (0530-0900) and evening window (1700-1930).  Weather mostly cooperated, except for heavy rain that cut morning survey short on May 9.

Results
We identified 42 species (compared to 37 same time last year).  Total individual detections was 1184.  Highlights / notables:

Virginia Rail - Identified at Station 3 on 4 occasions - possibly a pair for breeding.  Confirmed last in 2019.
Prothonotary warbler -  1 male singing at Station 6 - May 11, May 13.  Flagged for nest box assessment
Great Blue Heron - Active rookery near north dike with at least 6 occupied nests.
Swamp sparrows and common yellowthroats still the most common - ~22% of all detections.

Not all stations equally abundant - Stations 3 and 6 - 38% total detections.
Probably due to additional emergent marsh habitat after hydrology restoration this past fall.

All data entry complete in ebird and internal Northline database.
Need to review audio recorded on ARU devices at Stations 2 and 7.  J. Reyes to review by May 22.

Issues and Recommendations
1) Boardwalk from station 4 to station 5 is in disrepair.  2 planks loose.  Recommend maintenance prior to June round of surveys.
2) Mosquitoes are bad this year.  Recommend team members bring insect repellant for the rest of the spring counts.
3) Based on Prothonotary warbler detection, recommend placing 2 nest boxes near station 6 prior to June 1.

Next Steps
2nd round of surveys - June 3-12
Team assignments to be distributed by May 27
Questions - email me d.whitfield@northlineaudubon.org

FIELD RESEARCH LOG - BIRD POPULATION COUNTS CEDAR SWAMP
Week of May 6 -15, 2024
Submitted By Dana Whitfield - Field Technician. Northline Audubon Society

SUMMARY OF ACTIVITY
3 Person team (D.Whitfield, M.Okafor and intern J. Reyes). 10 consecutive days of surveys. 40 point count surveys of the Cedar Swamp monitoring grid. This included all 8 established station. Survey conducted during the AM (0530-0900) and PM(1700 -1930). Weather was good (only the May 9 AM (heavy rain) restricted survey).

RESULTS
We documented 42 species (compare to 37 from same time last year). Total detections (all individuals): 1184. Some highlights/notables;
1) Virginia rail - we have 4 detections at station 3. We may have a pair breeding. Last seen in 2019
2) Prothonotary warbler. 1 male singing on May 11 & 13 at station 6. Need to evaluate nest boxes.
3) Great blue Heron - active rookery near the north dike. At least 6 nests occupied.
4) Swamp sparrow and common yellowthroat are still the most common. Together they make up about 22% of detections

The bird abundance was not distributed equally across the station. A large proportion (38%) of the detections were at station 3 and 6. Likely due to the added emergent marsh that came with last fall's hydrology restoration.

All of the data has been entered into ebird and our internal northline database.
The autonomous recording unit (ARU) audio at station 2 and 7 need to be reviewed. (J. Reyes will be doing that by 5/22).

ISSUES/RECOMMENDATIONS
1) Boardwalk from station 4 to 5 is showing signs of wear. 2 loose planks. Recommend maintenance prior to the June survey.
2) Lots of mosquitoes this year. Bring bug spray for the rest of spring surveys.
3) We have a prothonotary warbler so I recommend putting out 2 nest boxes near station 6 prior to June 1.

NEXT STEPS
Our next survey window is June 3 -12. We will send out the team assignments by 5/27. Any questions feel free to contact me. d.whitfield@northlineaudubon.org

Maintenance Log Summary Tower B - Elevator 3

Elevator 3 (Tower B (Floors 1-14) was put out of service on Wednesday, Feb 12 @ 7:45am, due to intermittent door close issues, and hard stop per floor 9 tenant. Facilities Tech Raymond Ortiz performed initial diagnostics for the elevator that afternoon and the likely issues were identified as the door interlock contacts being worn, and main drive sheave bearing is going out.

We called in service to Almeida Elevator Co. the same day. Dana Whitfield (tech for Almeida) performed inspection on Feb 13 and confirmed the above issues. Additionally, door operator belt has excessive cracking and we need to proactively replace it.

On Feb 13, we ordered replacement parts, received them on Feb 17. Parts ordered are 1 drive sheave bearing assembly #SB-4471 1 door interlock contact set #DI-2209 1 door operator belt #DB-118

We did the replacement/installations on Feb 18. Elevator was locked out from 8:00am - 4:30pm

Dana Whitfield (Almeida) and Raymond Ortiz (Facilities Tech) conducted post installation testing on Feb 18-19, including full run with load and 50 door cycles. Passed all safety testing.

Unit was brought back into service on Thursday, Feb 19 at 11:00am. So it was out of service for 7 days.

Total cost for parts/labor was $3240 (covered under current service contract for building with Almeida Elevator Co.) No additional invoice to property.

Signage placed at all Tower B Lobby entrances to inform tenants to use Elevator 1 & 2. Building management posted 2 tenant notices on Feb 12 and Feb 17 via resident portal. No safety/entrapment issues during out of service time frame.

Next Preventive Maintenance for Elevator 3 scheduled for May 2026 (regular quarterly inspection cycle)

review_product_01_glm.text:
⭐⭐⭐⭐ Trattoria Roma - The Carbonara is Worth It 

Went to Trattoria Roma on a Friday (3/14) rainy night, around 730. My sis and I were coming from a Cubs game. They told us it would be a 25min wait. We ended up waiting about 15mins. Pretty good for Friday night. It is a very cute place. Exposed brick. Low lighting. It's a little loud but in a good way. Not a "can't hear each other" kind of loud. 
 But anyway, let's get to it, the carbonara. This is why I am writing this. The price was right for the area. It was $19.95. But it was much more. You could tell it was fresh, handmade pasta (just by texture). It was cooked a little after al dente. I know some purists will pucker their lips. But it was good. The sauce was nice and smooth. No cream. Just eggs yolks, pecorino and that goodness from the rendered guanciale. The pork itself was nice and big chunks with nice crispy edges. Not those pitiful bacon-like bits you see at other places. Also, a nice grind of black pepper giving it a nice kick. It was a nice size portion. I could not finish it. That's really saying something. 
 Our waiter was great. Good service but not too much. Our girl was Daniela. She was checking in at the right times. Filling up water glasses. Bread basket comes with a herbed olive oil dip. We tore that up while we waited. 
 Dislikes- the house Chianti ($9/glass) was kinda weak. The table kept wobbling. Our girl put a folded napkin under the leg. And street parking in this area is bad. Valet it up. 
 2 people. Split a tiramisu (awesome. Nice espresso kick). And drinks. $78 before tip. Good value for the quality. I will come back. I want to try the Cacio E Pepe.

⭐⭐⭐⭐ Trattoria Roma  - Must Visit For Carbonara

Visited Trattoria Roma (rainy Friday night) March 14th around 7:30 with my sister after the Cubs game. Quoted a wait time of 25 mins. Ended up getting a seat in about 15 mins. Not bad for a Friday. Place was very nice. Exposed brick, warm lighting, little loud (in a good way) not 'can't hear what you're saying' kind of loud. 

Ok, this is why I'm writing about this place. Carbonara. Carbonara! It's $19.95 which is right on par for the neighborhood. But wow! In execution this is amazing. You can tell by the texture that the pasta is made there. It's a little past al dente which I'm sure the 'purists' will go batshit over but it works. The sauce was very silky. No cream. Just egg yolk. Pecorino. That rendered guanciale goodness. The pork was in nice big chunks with crispy edges. Not like some wimpy little bacon bits you get at other places. Plenty of aggressive black pepper to round it out. The portion size was good. I didn't finish it. (And I rarely say that).

The service was good. Not overly attentive. Our server (Daniela) was there when you needed her. Keeping the glasses filled. Got a bread basket with herbed olive oil to dip. We ate that up while waiting. 

Only gripes are that the house Chianti ($9/glass) was a little weak. And the table wobbled. Daniela fixed it by putting a napkin under one leg. Also parking on the street in this area is crazy. You'll want valet. 

Bill for 2 w/shared tiramisu (excellent. Real espresso kick) and drinks. Came to $78 before tip. Good value for the quality. Will be back to try cacio e pepe.

 I got this in May (delivered May 14th) for $39.99 on Amazon. Looking for a reliable powerbank for 2 weeks trip in Portugal in June. Worked great for the first 3 months for me and able to fully charge my pixel 8 with 60% of the bank still available.
